Our team then modeled the necessary binding parameters of protein to albumin needed in order to create a feasible solution that would both reduce the overall amount of antibiotic used as well as the excess concentration in the blood.
igem_BNDS-China_2024: The human gut microbiota contains trillions of microorganisms, and it influences the human health from various aspects. Gut dysbiosis is caused when the balance of gut microbiota is disrupted, leading to disease conditions. In China, gut dieases and dysbiosis are becoming more prevalent, meaning the need for treatment. MetaboMender is designated to detect, monitor, and regulate the concentration of specific gut metabolites through a food input in order to cure and prevent gut dysbiosis. We designed two programmable genetic systems for beneficial and harmful metabolites. Both system use deoxycholic acid as an indicator of food intake to trigger the subsequent responses. We focused on butyrate and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) as the beneficial and harmful metabolites, respectively. When butyrate level is low, our platform will supplement butyrate by expressing butyrate-producing enzymes. On the other hand, when IAA level is too high, our platform will express IAA-degrading enzymes to reduce excessive IAA.
igem_KhanLabSchool_2024: Greenhouse gasses play a significant role in climate change, with carbon dioxide contributing to 79.7% of total emissions. However, while CO2 is abundant, it is not the most potent greenhouse gas. Methane has 86 times the warming impact of CO2 over 20 years yet comprising only 11.1% of emissions. Its severe environmental impact contributes to the formation of ground-level ozone, which damages crops and poses significant health risks. Thus, reducing methane emissions offers a more effective climate change strategy than focusing solely on CO2. Landfills are major methane sources, contributing to 17.1% of emissions in the United States. Our project aims to address this issue by genetically modifying the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis to produce enzymes that convert methane into compounds that boost soil fertility. This innovative approach reduces methane emissions while enhancing soil health.
igem_NU-Kazakhstan_2024: SanaGel is an innovative targeted ductal carcinoma bacteriotherapy developed using synthetic biology, ​​molecular biology, and materials science methods. The system comprises non-pathogenic Escherichia coli genetically engineered to produce a tumor-targeting peptide that selectively binds cell surfaces of cancer cells and forms pores, leading to tumor cell burst and eradication. Aside from the peptide's efficiency, we have implemented a Kill Switch (Suicide Gene) to ensure higher levels of safety control. Modified bacteria are encapsulated into agarose and chitosan-based hydrogel scaffolds, solidifying upon temperature rise after the intratumoral injection. Due to the careful fine-tuning of the gel's pores and sol-gel transition temperatures, hydrogels minimize bacterial leakage and ensure the system's local action. The project has the potential of opening the door to the development of novel sustainable cancer therapeutics that are not only efficient but also exhibit reduced systemic side effects on the healthy cells of patients.
igem_Squirrel-Shanghai_2024: The COVID pandemic has very serious consequences, killing more than 7 million people worldwide since its initiation in 2019. Despite the worldwide efforts leading to effective control of the pandemic, the continuous emergence of viral variants has necessitated the ongoing development of SARS-CoV-2 inhibitors. The main protease nsp5 plays a major role in the virus’s life cycle, and also serves as an important drug target for the virus. Our project primarily aims to develop an efficient and reliable in vivo nsp5 inhibitor screening system based on FlipGFP. Additionally, we also desire to investigate the possibility of using nsp5, a sequence-specific protease, as a tool enzyme for removing recombinant tags during protein purification
igem_Squirrel-CHN-II_2024: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a global concern, even with the implement of HBV vaccination. The current HBV detection is mainly blood serum-based, which is invasive, expensive and needs some waiting time to obtain the test results. Our project aims to develop a rapid, reliable, and low-cost detection system for HBV virus infection using the CRISPR/Cas12 and RPA technologies combined in one-pot assay to facilitate the screening and treatment of Hepatitis B disease.
igem_GEC-China_2024: AgroNeedle integrates synthetic biology with microneedle technology to deliver nutrients, pesticides, and antimicrobial agents directly to plants, revolutionizing agricultural practices. By enabling precise, localized delivery, this approach enhances the efficiency of nutrient and pesticide use while minimizing environmental impact, such as runoff and overuse of chemicals. The microneedles, designed for plant-specific applications, allow controlled release of agrochemicals, promoting sustainable farming practices. Additionally, leveraging synthetic biology enables the incorporation of advanced antimicrobial solutions, targeting plant pathogens effectively while reducing the reliance on traditional chemical treatments, contributing to healthier crops and ecosystems.
igem_RBHS-San-Diego_2024: UV radiation poses a threat to many populations, from astronauts to marine organisms, in the form of DNA damage in cells. Preventive measures have primarily focused on minimizing exposure to harmful UV rays. Sunscreen formulations, which contain UV-filtering compounds, represent a widely adopted approach to protect human skin. For our project, we decided to focus on maximizing the ability of photolyase to repair common types of DNA damage, particularly cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and pyrimidine-pyrimidone (6-4) photoproducts, within human skin cells. We plan to combine a cell penetrating peptide (specifically the TAT peptide from the HIV virus), a nuclear localization signal (from the SV40 Large T-antigen), and either a 6-4 photolyase protein (from Arabidopsis thaliana) or a CPD photolyase protein (from zebrafish) in one fusion protein, with linker sequences between each component to allow the protein to fold properly.
igem_XMU-China_2024: The rapid population growth has driven heavy demands for paper, leading to extensive deforestation and disturbing the ecological balance, thereby exacerbating the climate crisis. Enhancing the recycling of waste paper can mitigate deforestation, offering a significant contribution to addressing the climate crisis. Inspired by this, our project aims to investigate the current state and challenges of waste paper recycling in our REPARO project, we designed and developed an unprecedented deinking method based on synthetic biology, which could serve as a viable alternative to the chemical method on the industry scale. The implementation of our project holds immense potential to propel technological advancement and industrial upgrading within the waste paper recycling industry. Our project aims to introduce advanced biotechnology and environmental protection concepts to enhance the entire industry's production efficiency, product quality, and environmental protection level, thereby strengthening the industry's competitiveness and promoting the development of the circular economy.
igem_Aalto-Helsinki_2024: It is often said that if a medicine has no side effects, it's unlikely to work. Some of the most serious side effect causing drugs are chemotherapeutic drugs. COALES introduces a novel solution through targeted cancer therapy, leveraging Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation (LLPS) to enhance drug delivery precision. We aim to concentrate therapeutic agents like doxorubicin specifically, improving its effectiveness and reducing side effects. Traditional cancer therapies often result in severe toxicity and are costly, limiting access for many patients. With COALES, we hope to offer a more affordable, scalable, and accessible treatment alternative. COALES holds the potential to be adapted for various cancer types, offering an alternative to how cancer could be treated in the future. Throughout our project, we engaged in various activities related to Integrated Human Practices and Education to raise awareness and to obtain comprehensive knowledge.
igem_UChicago_2024: Schistosomiasis is a World Health Organization (WHO)-listed Neglected Tropical Disease characterized by the blood-dwelling helminths. Currently, all schistosomiasis vaccine candidates based on recombinant subunit antigens have encountered setbacks at various stages of clinical trials, underscoring the formidable challenges in vaccine development. Critically, these subunit vaccines lack the three-dimensional macrostructure necessary for optimal recognition by B cells as pathogenic. Drawing inspiration from Professor Mark Howarth’s group’s SpyCatcher-SpyTag system, a protein couple tool for peptide and protein ligation, our objective is to conjugate schistosomiasis antigens on virus-like-particle (VLP) scaffold to create high-density antigen nanoparticles to enhance vaccine immunogenicity. Together with a batch of novel antigens discovered in January 2024 through unbiased phage display, our aim is to present a diverse range of schistosomiasis antigens on VLPs. Thanks to the modularity of our VIPR, we hope to accelerate vaccine development and antigen screening for helminth diseases with a complex life cycle.
igem_Concordia-Montreal_2024: In a country built largely on resource extraction, mining continues to shape Canada’s landscapes and its people. Unfortunately, the impacts of mining cannot be ignored. Mine effluent – water originating from mine sites negatively impacts ecosystems and the communities living along contaminated waterways. Treating mining effluent is critical to maintain sustainable mining practices, conventional systems are often expensive and ineffective in reaching the small concentrations of contaminants required. We aim to sequester heavy metals from mining wastewater using a microbial process. A major problem with current mining practices is that they create highly acid environments that many organisms cannot tolerate. To create a bioremediation vector, we need to address the highly acidic environment that allows our microbe to be used in situ. While our initial goal is heavy metal sequestration, we are considering possible future methods for recovery of metals for circularity in the mining industry.
igem_TUPLS-Japan_2024: In recent years, initiatives like the Artemis Project have explored the potential for extraterrestrial resource acquisition and human habitation. However, due to the detrimental effects of space radiation and ultraviolet light, conventional microorganisms struggle to survive, necessitating a synthetic biology approach that is radiation-resistant. Our project addresses the critical challenge of energy production in space, proposing a solution through synthetic biology. We engineered Shewanella, an electrochemically active bacterium, by incorporating the ENEducer mechanism to not only protect it from radiation but also convert that radiation into usable energy. Additionally, a kill switch was integrated for biosafety. This system offers promising potential for developing microorganisms capable of producing valuable substances in space while converting radiation into energy, with broad applicability across various microbial species.
igem_MIT-MAHE_2024: Coffee Leaf Rust (CLR), caused by Hemileia vastatrix, severely impacts global coffee production, threatening farmers' livelihoods. Our project addresses CLR by enhancing the production of Iturin A, an antifungal lipopeptide from Bacillus subtilis ATCC 13952. Using homologous recombination, we aim to replace the native Iturin operon promoter with a stronger dual-promoter to boost Iturin A synthesis. This modification will be integrated into the chromosomal DNA of B. subtilis for stability. Additionally, we are developing a machine learning model that predicts coffee yields by analyzing historical data and environmental conditions. By offering a sustainable alternative to chemical fungicides, our approach not only targets CLR directly but also minimizes environmental harm. This project has the potential to protect coffee crops, improve farmers’ livelihoods, and serve as a model for addressing other agricultural diseases through genetic interventions.
igem_HunanU_2024: To reduce the difficulty of mammalian virus engineering in synthetic biology, we have successfully created an easy-to-customize viral chassis, named Click Virus, based on the principles of artificial translation and click reaction. Click Virus is a genetically engineered vaccinia virus with modified A27L membrane protein containing three 4-azido-L-phenylalanine (AzF) residues. To incorporate the unnatural amino acid AzF to A27L, we mutated three phenylalanine codons to amber suppressor codons (TAG) which were then translated into AzF by an artificial translation system involving amber suppressor tRNA and azidophenylalanine-specific tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase. The azido groups can be covalently linked to any customized molecules via click reactions of azido and dibenzocyclooctyne (DBCO), to obtain different engineered viruses for a wide variety of applications, such as targeting delivery of genes, oncolytic virus and vaccine carrier. Using folate-linked Click Virus, we achieved the directed infection to cells overexpressing folate receptors, preliminarily verifying the reliability of Click Virus.
igem_UnivLyon1-INSALyon_2024: Given global challenges like food insecurity and environmental degradation, it’s needed to protect agriculture and households from harmful insects to reduce food waste. BioSnare addresses this problem by developing a 100% bio-based and biodegradable adhesive patch designed to capture pests. Using a co-culture of Komagataeibacter rhaeticus, a cellulose-producing bacterium, and genetically modified Saccharomyces cerevisiae, our system produces functionalized cellulose equipped with adhesive properties and specific colors to attract target pests. The yeast is engineered to secrete a fusion of the barnacle-derived protein Cp19k and spider silk-derived Masp1 for strong adhesion, alongside yellow chromoprotein fwYellow to attract insects like the Suzuki fly. Cellulose-binding domains (CBD) ensure that these proteins adhere to the cellulose matrix, creating a biodegradable trap. BioSnare provides a versatile concept promising alternative to conventional insecticides and traps, which pollute the environment. It aims to protect agriculture and households while promoting environmental sustainability.
igem_PennState_2024: Gene-circuit-based sensors have significantly advanced medical diagnostics by enabling sensitive and specific biomarker detection. However, developing point-of-care diagnostics that are timely, cost-effective, and minimally invasive remains challenging. Our project, ROSA (Riboswitch Operated Sensor Apparatus), addresses this by creating a versatile, proof-of-concept detection method applicable in various medical settings. We engineered a riboswitch-based system to detect the biomarker CA125, demonstrating the simplicity and adaptability of novel riboswitch development. The biosensor functions in a cell-free system, where trehalase expression catalyzes the hydrolysis of excess trehalose into glucose, which can then be quantified using a standard glucose meter. This glucose meter-based reporting mechanism underscores the potential for adaptable, point-of-care diagnostics with broad applications in healthcare.
igem_CCA-San-Diego_2024: Fire Blight, an infectious disease caused by gram-negative bacteria Erwinia Amylovora devastates Rosaceae plants, including apple and pear trees. Our team proposes the use of darobactin, a novel antibiotic discovered to inhibit gram-negative bacteria by acting on the BamA protein by Yu Imai et al. at Northeastern University in 2019. We are the first to test darobactin on E. Amylovora and to design an infection-sensitive plasmid so that in the event of an E. Amylovora infection, the plasmid will be triggered by an infection-sensitive promoter to express the darABCDE operon that encodes for darobactin A production. Our goal is to explore the use of a P. agglomerans plasmid to express darobactin A to target E. amylovora in Rosaceae plants.
igem_DUESSELDORF_2024: Project KlothY focuses on developing a modular system to synthesise a textile fabric made of bacterial cellulose produced by Komagataeibacter xylinus. K. xylinus was genetically modified, to be able to regulate cellulose production. To modify the properties of the cellulose fabric, Saccharomyces cerevisiae acts as producer of metabolites, which impact flexibility and colour of our final product. We worked on integrating plant genes involved in hemicellulose biosynthesis and modified chromoproteins. Three chromoproteins attached to a cellulose binding domain would be used, to dye our fabric in a range of colours based on the CMY color model, also used in printers. The goal for the project is to contribute to the reduction of the harmful environmental impact of textile production globally, by focusing on local production and cutting down on the need for pesticides, emissions through transportation, high water usage and environmental toxic pollutants, used in bleaching and coloring processes.
igem_OhioState_2024: Polyethylene related plastic pollution is a serious environmental problem in Ohio, where just 2% of plastic waste is recycled. A potential solution is mycoremediation, which makes use of fungi's capacity for substrate degradation. The laccase enzyme of Pleurotus ostreatus, which has the ability to degrade polyethylene polymers, is the main focus of the MycoBite project. Our objective was to enhance the thermal stability and affinity of laccase on PE surfaces by utilizing a combined computational method that included protein engineering and enzymatic and molecular modeling. We suggest using Saccharomyces cerevisiae to express the optimized laccase, promoting increased enzyme activity while supporting creative approaches to the management of plastic waste and environmental sustainability. MycoBite hopes to offer a novel solution to PE bioremediation and contribute to sustainable waste management practices.
igem_ULaval_2024: Type 1 Hereditary Tyrosinemia (HT1) is a genetic disorder caused by mutations disabling the activity of the fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) protein, crucial for tyrosine metabolism.  While nitisinone is the standard treatment for the disease, it imposes significant dietary restrictions, leading to dissatisfaction among patients surveyed from the Groupe d’Aide aux Enfants Tyrosinémiques du Québec (GAETQ). Tyro Tweezers proposes an FAH enzyme replacement therapy to complement nitisinone. After consulting with experts, we chose a subcutaneous injection strategy for delivery. We attempted to express human FAH in E. coli but we encountered challenges and unfortunately failed to produce a recombinant plasmid with the FAH gene.  We aimed to optimize the ligand-protein binding affinity. We performed molecular dynamics simulations on FAH. 26 candidate mutations were identified by bioinformatics tools. We planned to use Rosetta Flexddg to compute the binding affinities for each mutated protein but time constraints prevented us from conducting the analyses.
igem_UCSC_2024: The 2024 UCSC iGEM project, LiFT (Limnospira-inspired Foundational Technologies), aims to advance cyanobacteria engineering using new technology we call "accelerators." Limnospira fusiformis (SAG 85.79) is a promising chassis for developing nutrient-rich, cost-effective infant formula, addressing global malnutrition and high formula costs. While initially focused on creating a genetic system in L. fusiformis, Synechococcus sp. (UTEX 3154) was chosen for its well-characterized bio-engineering pathways. To overcome the lengthy transformation processes caused by polyploidy and restriction-modification systems, we remove restriction sites using statistical testing. Modular cloning is employed to build accelerator plasmids, including Cas12a and Argonaute, to speed up genetic recombination. Our project involves three accelerator designs: Cas12a single plasmid, Cas12a double plasmid, and Argonaute double plasmid. The UCSC iGEM team aims to apply this research to L. fusiformis in the future, creating a foundation for efficient cyanobacteria engineering.
igem_TecCEM_2024: In Mexico, where 1 in 6 adults is affected by type 2 diabetes and food insecurity remains a significant challenge, the iGEM TEC CEM team presents ALEBBRIGE: Active Linked Edible Biopeptides in B. subtilis: Recombinant Integrated Genetic Engineering, a cutting-edge recombinant dietary supplement developed to assist in the prevention of diabetes and its associated complications. Drawing inspiration from Mexico's vibrant alebrijes, ALEBBRIGE integrates a diverse array of bioactive protein peptides, designed to provide precise nutritional support. By leveraging the capabilities of Bacillus subtilis as an efficient system for protein production, our multipeptide supplement aims to enhance metabolic health and support the prevention of diabetes-related conditions.
igem_NYCU-Formosa_2024: Early detection of diseases is crucial to ensure timely treatment and avoid severe outcomes. To address this, we developed CHELO, a device capable of detecting multiple diseases using biosensors. We focused on leukemia, where hematopoietic stem cells abnormally proliferate, affecting the patient's health. Each year, around 29,000 adults and 2,000 children are diagnosed with leukemia, with acute cases progressing rapidly and requiring early detection. Our project identifies biomarkers for AML using our model, Artemis' Eye. We discovered CD97 as a key biomarker and designed short peptides that bind to it. These peptides are expressed on our engineered E. coli, BELO. When CD97 binds to these peptides, BELO emits an electrical signal, indicating detection. This system alerts users to potential disease risks, enabling prompt medical attention. In the future, we aim to optimize the peptides, broaden disease detection, and enhance accuracy, helping patients worldwide receive timely treatment.
igem_HongKong-JSS_2024: Our project tackles heavy metal contamination in Hong Kong, inspired by incidents like lead in public housing water and contaminations from various origins such as agricultural land pollution, misconnection of pipes, and sewage water pouring into storm drains. These concerns highlight the need for affordable, user-friendly biosensors to detect metals like lead, cadmium, mercury, and zinc. To ensure visual detection in our biosensors, we focused on using chromoprotein reporters. Then, we identified metal-inducible promoters from literature and the iGEM database, studied their characteristics, and integrated them with the chromoprotein reporter system. We successfully developed a lead biosensor and a cadmium biosensor and demonstrated that the lead biosensor is concentration-sensitive. Additionally, our hardware team developed an automated machine using IoT and AI technologies. It can cultivate the biosensors and features an automated detection and warning system, ensuring practical and accessible monitoring of heavy metal pollutants in various settings.
igem_Cambridge_2024: Spatiotemporal gene control is a crucial technique utilised by academics in a variety of fields, ranging from neuroscience to stem cell research. However, the tools available for the control of gene expression in cell-based systems are limited - whether by timescale, spatial resolution, cost, or a combination of the three. To overcome these limitations, we have designed our MaGenTa technology: a spatiotemporal targeting system capable of activating gene expression using a combination of magnetic fields, magnetic nano particles (MNPs) and genetic AND gates. Our system relies on the activation of cellular pathways that function independently from one another. For this, we identified 3 viable pathways: thermal, mechanical and magnetic.
igem_IIT-Madras_2024: One of the grand challenges in space synthetic biology is in situ resource utilization (ISRU). This eliminates the need to transport materials from Earth, which can be expensive and cumbersome. Another challenge is the manufacture of valuable compounds, like platform chemicals and pharmaceuticals, in space. We present a novel co-culture system of silicon-solubilizing bacteria (Pseudomonas fluorescens) and diatoms (Phaeodactylum tricornutum) that can use the silica present in Martian soil to drive their growth and produce compounds of human interest. As a proof-of-concept, we have engineered our bacterium to produce 4(S)-limonene. We also present Astrolabe, a first-of-its-kind software for applications in space synthetic biology and biomanufacturing.
igem_CSU-CHINA_2024: Glycemic Stabilizer is a treatment project for type 1 diabetes patients. We have designed an AND part that can secrete insulin to reduce blood glucose during high blood glucose levels. To prevent low blood glucose, we have also designed a NOT part that can block excessive insulin secretion in a timely manner, thereby achieving precise regulation of blood glucose levels. We validated the feasibility of the plan through biological experiments. We also conducted social research and promoted knowledge of synthetic biology. In addition, we constructed a scientific model which is visualized of the project, designed user-friendly software with practical value and educational significance, and developed a blue light instrument which is successfully applied in experiments.
igem_Jiangnan-China_2024: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic pollution poses a global environmental issue, and enzymatic degradation is an ideal ecologically friendly solution, yet its efficiency is restricted by limited substrate accessibility of corresponding enzymes. Therefore, our project applied the STROM strategy to boost the degradation ability of PETase towards PET by PET-binding peptides. Initially, sixteen potential PET-binding peptides were screened using deep learning models. Subsequently, fusion proteins of these PET-binding peptides with PETase were constructed to test PET microplastic degradation and binding efficiency, identifying three efficient peptides. Through optimization, the expression levels and PET degradation properties of these fusion proteins were further enhanced. Finally, with the aid of the Mutcompute-super model, these three peptides were re-modified, further improving the expression levels and PET microplastic degradation efficiencies of their fusion proteins, with the optimal degradation efficiency reaching 207.49% of PETase. Our project provides insights and support for the biodegradation of PET plastics.
igem_HKUST_2024: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is an essential nutrient needed for human health and development, however, dietary intake is proven insufficient in many populations. Current DHA supplement sources include fish oil and microalgae, in which the former is susceptible to pollution and predicted to decline in productivity due to global warming, and the latter faces high production costs. To provide an alternative method of efficient and sustainable DHA production, our team selects oleaginous yeast Yarrowia lipolytica, a safe, commonly used organism for industrial fatty acid production as our chassis. We integrate the gene cluster encoding a specific DHA-synthesizing enzyme complex from Schizochytrium sp. into the yeast’s genome. We then apply the following strategies to optimize the DHA yield: peroxisomal PEX10 gene knockout by homologous recombination to inhibit DHA degradation; control of gene expression level and production stages via promoter characterization and design; replenishing reactant NADPH supply through GapC gene introduction.
igem_SZU-China_2024: With increasing concerns over the health risks associated with excessive sugar consumption, the use of sugar substitutes has become widespread. However, recent studies have identified significant safety issues with many common substitutes. In response, the SZU-China team seeks to develop a safer alternative by producing Thaumatin, a natural, highly efficient, and fully digestible sweet protein. We have implemented an innovative production method within tomato fruits, utilizing two key systems: an expression system driven by the fruit-specific and ripening-induced E8 promoter for precise temporal and spatial control of Thaumatin production, and a storage-targeting system that directs Thaumatin to the vacuole using the SPS-NTPP targeting peptide. This approach enables the direct extraction of Thaumatin from tomato juice, eliminating the need for complex purification processes. We have named this protein 'Sweetein' and hope it will inspire further advancements in the sugar substitute industry by offering safer, natural alternatives for consumers.
igem_LZU-MEDICINE-CHINA_2024: We are concerned about T2DM, a chronic disease with serious complications and a rising incidence rate worldwide. We focus on BcoAT to enhance the synthesis of its SCFAs and program the glucose responsive secretion of GLP-1 to build a synthetic biological reactor through the method of synthetic biology, with the probiotic ECN1917 as the chassis. When blood sugar levels rise after each meal, GLP-1 is released to rapidly lower blood sugar to baseline levels. In order to achieve the above functions, this project designed a GLP-1 recombinant protein, with PelB as the lead sequence connected to GLP-1 to enhance its extracellular secretion function. DnaK, a key protein of the blood glucose control module, is expressed at the tail of GLP-1 through flexible linker peptides to achieve its programmed release. During the experimental phase, the release of GLP-1 regulated by glucose concentration was validated through gradient dilution and ELISA quantitative detection.
igem_HKSSC_2024: Leptospira, a genus of motile gram-negative spirochetes, causes leptospirosis, a zoonotic disease that significantly impacts resource-poor populations. Transmitted through contaminated environments, it affects high-risk groups like agricultural workers and water sports enthusiasts. Clinical manifestations range from mild flu-like symptoms in anicteric leptospirosis to severe complications in icteric leptospirosis (Weil’s disease). The complement system is crucial for immune defense; however, some Leptospira proteins evade it, complicating host responses. Recent studies have identified specific microRNAs (miRNAs), such as hsa-miR-144-3p and hsa-miR-21-5p, which down-regulate important immune components, including toll-like receptors and complement factor H. This project aims to investigate the interaction between these miRNAs and their targets to design synthetic miRNA mimics/inhibitors. The goal is to enhance the immune response, particularly TLR2 and complement factor H activity, improving defenses against leptospirosis. Over two years, this research seeks to provide insights into potential therapeutic strategies for managing the disease and its complications.
igem_NASSZ_2024: The NASSZ iGEM team, in its inaugural year, aimed to address a common issue among secondary students: sleep difficulties. Through surveys, the team identified problems with falling asleep and waking up refreshed. To tackle this, they proposed using aromatherapy, focusing on mint and vanilla scents to enhance focus and sleep quality. The team plans to engineer yeast to synthesize menthol and vanillin using recombinant DNA techniques. Additionally, they are designing a light-sensitive system where yeast would produce menthol or vanillin based on exposure to red or blue light. A device with a timer will allow students to switch between scents for better sleep and focus.
igem_UniMuenster_2024: Mosquitoes are the single most deadly animal to humans due to their role as vectors for parasitic and viral diseases. The least polluting method of controlling this epidemic is the use of insect repellents. However, their current production relies on petroleum and toxic intermediates, posing a major threat to the environment. So, we developed a biosynthetic pathway to produce a promising alternative to current repellents: NBP. We designed and partially constructed an enzyme cascade to produce NBP from sugar feedstocks. To improve the catalytic activity of our key enzyme, we devel-oped the software tool 'seq-mutator', which bridges the gap between AI-assisted protein engineering and real-world data, ultimately resulting in a variant with about a five-fold increase in activity. We also explored the use of black pepper as a sustainable production chassis by developing novel transformation protocols, and by producing NBP in Nicotiana benthamiana as proof of concept.
igem_Concordia-Shanghai_2024: The ketogenic diet offers numerous benefits, including enhanced cognitive function, improved exercise performance, and appetite suppression, making it attractive for weight management and athletic performance. However, its requirements for low carbohydrate intake and prolonged fasting render it impractical for most individuals. To address this limitation, we have engineered E. coli to biosynthesize d-β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), a ketone body, which can substitute the need for a strict ketogenic diet to reach ketosis. Our modified bacteria first produce the polymer poly hydroxybutyrate (PHB), which is then converted to BHB through the expression of PHB depolymerase. Through rigorous testing, we successfully detected BHB production from our engineered cells, demonstrating the feasibility of our system. By facilitating easier access to the benefits of ketosis without dietary constraints, our project capitalizes on the recent development of safe and orally bioavailable ketone monoester drinks, highlighting a significant market opportunity.
igem_BIT-China_2024: In the 21st century, climate and energy issues have increased the demand for lithium-ion batteries. Yet, their disposal poses safety and environmental risks, and metal scarcity highlights the need for recycling. Conventional recycling is inefficient and polluting. We propose a synthetic biology approach to recover metals (Li, Mn, Co, Ni) from used batteries. A. niger ferments to produce acids for metal leaching, yeast displays peptides to selectively bind and separate ions, and E. coli's urease helps precipitate ions as carbonates for new anode production, creating a sustainable metal recovery loop.
igem_HUBU-WUCHANG-CHINA_2024: Strategically, we utilize the dose-response of rice genes and the transcriptome regulatory network of endosperm storage protein synthesis genes to guide the reprogramming of rice endosperm storage protein component protein ratios through modeling and prediction. We only mutate the coding genes of two storage proteins without introducing any exogenous genes to improve the nutritional quality, food safety, and taste quality of rice. Technically, we induced rice polyploidy to tetraploid by colchicine, and then mutated glutelin B1 and globulin coding genes OsGluB1 and OsGlb by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology. As a result, the total protein and lysine content were increased (improving nutritional quality); The content of glutelin remained basically unchanged, and globulin almost disappeared (food safety was improved); Increased alcohol soluble protein content (improved taste quality).
igem_SMS-Shenzhen_2024: Bananas, being triploid and reliant on asexual reproduction, lack genetic diversity, making them highly susceptible to pathogens like Fusarium oxysporum, which threatens entire banana industury. Traditional sterilization methods (sunlight, chemical disinfectants, soil isolation) are ineffective and unsustainable. Instead, our project focuses on coexistence through competition. We genetically modify Fusarium oxysporum by removing the FUB1 toxin gene and introducing the RiCLE symbiotic gene from Rhizophagus irregularis, creating a strain that promotes banana growth while protecting against wild-type pathogens. The modified fungus acts as a vaccine, occupying ecological niches to fend off harmful strains. To prevent biohazard, we designed a kill switch system using tetracycline to control spore production within a specialized fermentation tank. Spores are produced safely. Waste water is disinfected with disinfectant and air is disinfected with filter membrane and UV light, ensuring controlled and bio-safe application. Our final product is a spore suspension kit with dry spore powder.
igem_IISc-Bengaluru_2024: We produced recombinant hTau in BL21 E. coli culture. The purified Tau was randomly phosphorylated to match the levels of phosphorylation in case of Tauopathies and collected at different intervals of incubation (18 hrs, 22 hrs, 24 hrs, 27 hrs etc). The phosphorylations were confirmed by band shifts. Using a variant of EMSA, we showed the binding of the Aptamers to 231 pTau. Parallelly, we clicked C8 alkyne dCTP and [S,R,S]-AHPC-PEG1-Azide. This versatile compound is theoretically expected to be incorporable into Aptamers making an aptamer-based PROTAC, but our algorithmic calculation of radius of gyration showed the possibility of a coiled moiety. We also tried to establish a newer protocol of SELEX by optimising an improvised random mutagenesis protocol. We also obtained various structural predictions of pTau for different combinations of phosphorylation on majorly addressed phosphorylation sites.
igem_Anatolia-College_2024: Concerned about plastic pollution in our city Thessaloniki and its global impact we decided to tackle this problem using synthetic biology. Our projects includes creating a fused enzyme, by the two enzymes: PETase from Ideonella Sakaiensis and cutinase from Humicola Insolens, in order to accelerate the rate and efficiency of PET biodegradation. This fused enzyme was expressed in E. Coli through TA Gene cloning in pMiniT 2.0 vector. We tested our project using gel electrophoresis and spectrophotometry.
igem_Sheffield_2024: Modern agriculture relies on the availability of synthetic fertilizers to feed an ever-growing global population. Unfortunately, one of the key components of these fertilizers, inorganic phosphate (Pi) is a finite resource that the world is set to run out of in the coming decades. This impending "Phosphogeddon" crisis will require new methods for recycling phosphate. We propose that phosphatase enzymes like PafA from Flavobacterium johnsoniae will allow us to recycle naturally-occurring organophosphates found in soil. First we set out to characterize PafA, then employed AI-guided protein redesign tools to enhance its expression, stability, and industry-readiness. By deploying our phosphatase with a high-affinity phosphate binding protein (PiBP) in a future waste-water treatment system, we can both effectively convert organophosphates back into inorganic phosphate and captured it for reuse. Overall, our project addresses the looming threat of "phosphogeddon" by both introducing a new source of inorganic phosphate and method for its capture
igem_EHSBNU_2024: Horseshoe crabs currently face extinction due to blood harvest for medical research. Sourcing natural horseshoe crab hemolymph, which is involved in endotoxin and fungal infection detection systems, are therefore ecologically unsustainable. In this study, we recombinantly produced Tachypleus tridentatus clotting factor G, a heterodimeric protein consisting of alpha and beta subunits, to reconstruct the (1→3)-β-D-glucans (BDG) assay system for fungal infection. We optimized and cloned the alpha and beta subunit sequences into pET-28a, pET-Duet1, and pFastBac1 vectors, hoping to express them in both Escherichia coli and Sf9 insect cells. Assay with SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry indicated the successful expression of both subunits in E.coli cells. The protein would then be purified and tested for BDG-dependent activation. Our findings contribute to the development of alternative diagnostic tools for fungal infection while addressing ecological concerns.
igem_Shanghaitech-China_2024: Itchiness, or pruritus, is a common discomfort that can escalate into a persistent and challenging issue when caused by specific factors like Staphylococcus aureus. This pathogen not only leads to inflammation and redness but also triggers relentless itching, severely affecting the quality of life. The itch disrupts daily activities, sleep, and emotional well-being, often leading to anxiety and depression. Current anti-itch products, mostly focused on antibiotics and medications, don't always provide quick or significant relief and may have side effects like skin thinning and pigmentation. Recognizing the urgency and importance of this issue, we are committed to using Escherichia coli as a model to simulate the itch caused by Staphylococcus aureus and identify effective substances to alleviate the discomfort. Our goal is to develop a safe, user-friendly product that soothes itching and aids in treatment without interfering with conventional methods, providing a more comfortable and pleasant experience for those affected.
igem_HUST-China_2024: As plastic use escalates, agriculture faces increasing threats from microplastics, which originate from films, irrigation, wastewater, and compost. These particles compromise soil structure and quality, leading to reduced crop yields and altering crucial properties such as bulk density and water retention. More severely, crops may absorb these microplastics, impairing their ability to take up nutrients and water effectively. To combat these alarming issues, we introduce PETlizer—a groundbreaking solution featuring engineered E. coli BL21 to break down microplastics and Pseudomonas putida KT2440 to convert the byproducts into rhamnolipids. Rhamnolipids are powerful surfactants that enhance microbial adhesion, improve soil water retention, inhibit pathogens, and assist in pollution remediation. We hope this innovative approach will not only address plastic contamination but also boost agricultural productivity.
igem_Chalmers-Gothenburg_2024: In recent years, there has been a rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) at a global scale. Therefore, it is of great importance to develop new strategies to combat infections caused by antimicrobial resistant bacteria. The aim of this project is to develop a detection system utilizing toehold switches, and to establish an RNA-based gene silencing system. The ambition was to create and examine the efficacy of four different RNA-based silencing systems: sRNA, hammerhead RNA, CRISPR/Cas9, and CRISPR/Cas13a. Three antibiotic resistance genes, AAC(6’)-Ib, ErmC, and Tet(A), were chosen for the purpose of testing these systems. Our results demonstrate that the sRNA system successfully represses the expression of ErmC and Tet(A), restoring the susceptibility of these bacteria to antibiotic treatment. Additionally, we explored a novel approach of transforming plasmid DNA using graphene oxide.
igem_Manchester_2024: How can synthetic biology revolutionise our connections to machines? Our bodies use electrical signals for cellular communication, and myoelectric prosthetics can translate electrical signals generated from muscle contractions in the residual limb into movement using dry metal electrodes. However, a critical limiting factor for these electrodes is the overreliance on direct contact with the skin, making them vulnerable to interference from sweat and movement. This results in the electrodes moving out of place, leading to inaccurate signal interpretation (motion artefacts), causing lagging limb movement. We aim to improve the electrode’s interface using electrically conductive pili (e-pili) derived from Geobacter sulfurreducens. By combining the e-pili’s PilA monomer with a skin-specific protein-binding tag on the carboxy-terminal end, we will create nanowires that adhere to the skin surface. These nanowires would decrease the distance electrical signals would need to travel without a conductor, minimising motion artefacts and improve signal detection in human–machine interfaces.
igem_Virginia_2024: Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency (EPI) is a condition where the pancreas fails to produce sufficient digestive enzymes, leading to malnutrition. It is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, an oral drug containing porcine-derived pancreatic enzymes. As a more ethical and economic treatment option, we present the Bacillus Lipase Integrated Secretion System (BLISS), a probiotic that secretes synthetic digestive enzymes suitable for the human body. We plan to transform B. subtilis with the human pancreatic lipase and procolipase genes, along with a glucose-mediated switch mechanism for inducible expression. We have also developed a comprehensive model to determine the timescale of enzyme production and secretion. Our device also contains a biocontainment mechanism to prevent the device from functioning in unintended environments. In addition to our wet lab efforts, our team has developed a comprehensive education handbook as a synthetic biology resource for the homeschooled community.
igem_William-and-Mary_2024: As synthetic biology advances from the lab to real-world environments, it is in need of novel parts, circuits, and devices that increase levels of control in unpredictable, complex conditions. Satellite phages present a vast ensemble of unexplored machinery with the potential to meet these emerging needs. Our project, SaPh:IRES (Satellite Phage: Integrated Real-world Engineering Solutions), addresses the significant foundational gap  by pursuing two key objectives: developing novel identification tools for satellites both bioinformatically and experimentally, and utilizing their unique mechanisms to address specific challenges in synthetic biology. To do so, we use different phage satellite systems in mycobacteria and E. coli for three specific applications: sequence-specific population level control, overcoming prophage immunity, and increasing phage host range. We test our concepts in silico with the first of its kind mathematical model, in vitro, and in situ in simulated real-world environments to showcase their functionality at different levels of complexity.
igem_Princeton_2024: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the colon, affecting 5 million people worldwide with increasing incidence. Current treatments, targeting periods of remission and flare-ups, often fall short, with only 20-30% of patients seeing significant improvement. Our project, BOOMcoli, introduces a novel therapeutic model using bioengineered E. coli probiotics for targeted release of IL-10 in the colon. By utilizing a biomarker-sensitive promoter and quorum sensing, our engineered probiotic binds to inflamed sites identified by elevated calprotectin levels, an inflammation marker. Once localized, quorum sensing triggers synchronized lysis, releasing IL-10 precisely in the inflamed areas. BOOMcoli intends for a fast-acting, highly specific, and minimally invasive treatment that can be administered regularly to manage UC symptoms as they arise. Beyond UC, this method could be adapted for other large intestine diseases, including colorectal cancer, or other organs for broader therapeutic applications.
igem_IISER-TVM_2024: The fashion and cosmetics industries are highly consumer-centric, impacting nearly everyone worldwide. These industries consume vast quantities of raw materials and can significantly harm the environment. Indian sandalwood oil is one such sought-after raw material in the beauty industry. PETal presents a novel solution by integrating plastic waste management with the production of sandalwood oil, using synthetic biology. Using engineered Pseudomonas putida that can metabolise the monomers of polyethylene terephthalate (PET), i.e. terephthalic acid (TPA) and ethylene glycol (EG), we aim to synthesise santalene and santalol, the major components of sandalwood oil. This offers a sustainable alternative to conventional sandalwood oil extraction, reducing the strain on natural populations and providing a novel method for plastic upcycling. By creating a value-added product from PET plastic waste, PETal has the potential to reshape waste management strategies, promote biodiversity conservation, and simultaneously meet the global demands for sandalwood oil.
igem_SJTU-BioX-Shanghai_2024: Our project aims to develop a genetic switch that responds to ultraviolet (UV) light and utilize this gene switch for the treatment of Xeroderma Pigmentosum Type C. Our project is mainly divided into three modules: First, we verified the interaction of UVR8, COP1, and RUP2 in mammalian cells and their response to ultraviolet light; Second, we successfully constructed a UV-responsive gene switch that activates the expression of target genes upon UV irradiation and demonstrated that RUP2 can dissociate the interaction between UVR8 and COP1, thereby stabilizing the expression level of the target gene to a certain extent; Third, through modeling, we obtained results predicting the expression of the target protein after sequence optimization of RUP2, and successfully constructed plasmids with different numbers of rare codons added to the RUP2 gene, which will be validated through wet lab experiments.
igem_SWUer-China_2024: With the global incidence of fungal infections rising each year, over 300 million individuals are currently afflicted by severe fungal infections annually. The treatment success rate of antifungal drugs is only 67.4%, and the resistance is becoming increasingly critical. In response to this challenge, SWU-China team is focused on developing an innovative and efficient method for the high-throughput screening of antifungal peptides (AFP) utilizing deep learning techniques. The team employs the DeBERTa model to rapidly identify potential antifungal peptide sequence patterns from existing AFP data and predict the activity of candidate antimicrobial peptides from the NCBI database. Compared to conventional wet-lab methods, this model-driven approach offers significant improvements in both screening efficiency and accuracy. Through this project, we are committed to raising public awareness regarding fungal infections and antibiotic resistance. Simultaneously, we aim to provide novel solutions for medicine development, reducing the global health risks associated with fungal infections.
igem_GreatBay-SCIE_2024: Spider mites are notorious pests that destroys worldwide agriculture and horticulture. With abundant progenies and a short life cycle, they develop resistance to chemical pesticides at an exponential rate, making them difficult to exterminate using current strategies. Determined to resolve this global challenge, GreatBay-SCIE thus proposed a thorough solution called Dienamite, which shields plants at multiple stages including pre-, mid-, and post-infection stages. By bio-synthesizing 7-epi-zingiberene, 9-hydroxy-zingiberene, 9-hydroxy-10,11-epoxy zingiberene, mite venom peptide, spider venom peptide, and harpin protein, Dienamite is capable of establishing progeny-reducing effects on spider mites, exterminating adult mites with high target-specificity, and boosting plant immunity simultaneously. Ultimately, we wish to bring prosperity back to gardens and augment agricultural production. We also believe that the emergence of Dienamite can reduce reliance on chemical pesticides, minimizing toxic residues and preserving the environment.
igem_LINKS-China_2024: The global rise in wars and natural disasters increased the prevalence of wound infections. Moreover, the misuse of antibiotics and their resistance-prone mechanisms of action led to the spread of resistant pathogens that significantly increased the severity of infections, resulting in amputation or death. Current first aid kits do not possess any means of infection prevention other than resistant-prone antibiotic ointments. However, defensins, a family of antimicrobial peptides, possess antimicrobial activity while having lower risks of resistance due to their unique mechanisms of action. This year, we engineered a collection of fusion proteins capable of forming antimicrobial coatings on first aid kit items by attaching domains that could bind to a wide range of first-aid materials to defensins and developing an innovative release mechanism using the SUMO tag. We envision our resistance-free antimicrobial CuraPack to provide protection against infections in diverse scenarios and propagate first aid knowledge throughout the world.
igem_AIS-China_2024: Mosquitoes transmit various infectious diseases, such as malaria and dengue fever, and current control measures are often inadequate. While attractive targeted sugar baits (ATSBs) have shown promise, they are not sufficiently appealing to blood-feeding mosquitoes, the main disease vectors. AIS-China introduces Moskilla, an optimized ATSB enhancing attractiveness by incorporating HMBPP-producing E. coli and RNAi-based targeted shRNA mosquitocides. The engineered E. coli overproduces HMBPP through an enhanced MEP pathway and the use of sRNAs to downregulate the expression of downstream enzyme IspH, yielding 0.45 mM HMBPP, while shRNAs, produced in yeast, achieved a 100% mortality rate in mosquitoes within three days. To ensure biosafety, a kill switch using the ΦX174-E gene was developed for E. coli, enabling control outside laboratory settings. Moskilla, supported by a hardware device to limit GMOs use, represents an eco-friendly and effective solution for preventing and controlling mosquito-borne diseases, making it a promising innovation for our startup.
igem_Tsinghua_2024: As the incidence of IBD is increasing globally, the poor therapeutic experience, which the patients are required to receive long-term hormone injection and biologic combination therapy, is determined to seek a breakthrough. Our team stands to develop a more favorable treatment experience. Relevant studies have shown that lactic acid has an inhibitory effect on abnormally activated dendritic cells and cytotoxic T-cells in autoimmune diseases, and thus is expected to improve the symptoms of IBD patients. Based on the research, we designed a yeast engineered bacterium. We introduced a muscone detecting switch in the engineered yeast and activated the downstream pathway to express lactate dehydrogenase to produce lactic acid. Ultimately, the engineered bacteria will colonize the small intestine, enabling the patient to treat IBD by inhaling muscone gas in vitro therefore induces the yeast to synthesize a low amount of stabilized lactic acid in vivo.
igem_SubCat-Shanghai_2024: A subset of pregnant women is unable to metabolize folic acid into its active form, a deficiency that can result in congenital malformations. These women require supplementation with the active form of folic acid. However, the production of active folic acid is hindered by low yields, high costs, and potential food safety concerns. Our project seeks to overcome these challenges by using genetic engineering to develop bacterial strains capable of expressing the enzymes required to convert folate into its active form. This approach has the potential to enable large-scale biological production of active folate. In the future, our research may provide a viable health supplement for pregnant women with impaired folic acid metabolism.
igem_Beijing-HS_2024: According to statistics from the World Health Organization, there are about 280 million depression patients in the world. Among them, the depression of school-age teenagers is more serious. How to improve the condition of patients is a major problem currently faced. The content of propionate and acetate in the intestine is believed to be related to a variety of diseases, including depression. In this study, we modified the metabolic pathways of the probiotic ECN to increase the content of other short-chain fatty acids such as acetate and propionate, helping to confirm the possibility of incorporating this technology into human practice. In the future, our project could serve as a body regulator used in probiotic capsules to help individuals improve or alleviate the negative effects of depression.
igem_NNHS_2024: [Background] Gene mutations enhance biodiversity and agricultural benefits, but unpredictable mutagenesis methods pose risks, preventing their use in animals or humans. There are few methods available to introduce random mutations in specific genomic DNA regions without impacting other areas. [Design] We hypothesize that fusing Cytosine Base Editor (CBE) with blue-light-sensitive elements (p-Mag/n-Mag) and split T7 RNA polymerase (RNAP) could create a blue-light-controlled, DNA region-specific semi-random mutagenesis system. [Results] We used GFP as a real-time reporter and developed a fluorescent-based high-throughput screening workflow to select positive mutations. We applied the CBE-Mag-RNAP system to the NADPH, spermidine synthesis, and nicotinate degradation pathways in Escherichia coli. GFP-negative and selection-survived colonies, followed by next-generation sequencing, identified "gain of function" mutations. These enhanced Caenorhabditis elegans longevity through NADPH and spermidine pathways, while mutations in the nicotinate pathway restored lifespan in a high-nicotinate environment. [Conclusion] We established the CBE-Mag-RNAP mutagenesis system and a functional mutation library.
igem_UNC-ChapelHill_2024: Our team aims to develop a therapeutic protein designed to eliminate concentrations of perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), with a specific focus on targeting perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA). Our novel protein is designed to work by binding to PFOA in the bloodstream and then removing it by excretion into the mucosa. This involves engineering a novel chimeric protein with two domains: one has a high affinity for PFOA while the other facilitates transcytosis of the whole peptide. After binding to PFOA in the bloodstream, this protein will facilitate its transcytosis across epithelial cells for excretion via the mucosal lining.
igem_PuiChing-Macau_2024: Essential oils have been used widely in daily life products (such as shampoo and soap). Currently, 93% of essential oils are extracted with steam distillation. While this method does not involve toxic chemicals, the yield of essential oil extraction is very low, usually less than 2% of the plant materials.  Previous studies identified enzymes which could break down plant cell walls, increasing yield and preserving the quality of the oils. However, these enzymes are not stable during the boiling-hot steam distillation. We here used various engineered E. coli to produce thermostable enzymes (pectinase and cellulase) which allowed substantial enzyme activities during steam distillation, and significantly improved the yield. In addition, we produced lipases to esterify extracted oils, which enhanced their anti-bacterial properties. We also interacted with multiple industrial and academic partners, filed a patent, and designed hardware and models to ensure our project could be launched to the market shortly.
igem_UCalgary_2024: ErythrO2 addresses the global blood shortage by developing a strategy for the recombinant production of Lumbricus terrestris erythrocruorin (LtEc), an extracellular oxygen carrier found in earthworms, in order to contribute to the development of a shelf-stable, non-toxic, and efficient hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier (HBOC). Our project focused on cloning and expressing the six protein subunits comprising LtEc in a yeast and E. coli chassis—the first time this has been done.  We successfully cloned five subunits for expression in Pichia pastoris and four subunits for expression in E. coli. We achieved successful expression of one subunit in Pichia pastoris and three subunits in E. coli. Additionally, we designed a shuttle vector for recombinant expression in Pichia pastoris, which future teams can utilize for their synthetic biology projects.  In the dry lab, we tested linker truncation and established the possibility of a modified LtEc structure with higher binding efficiency.
igem_Stanford_2024: Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy (FSHD) is a rare neuromuscular disorder affecting approximately 1 in 12,000 people, causing progressive and highly variable loss of skeletal muscle, as well as debilitating pain and fatigue. The root cause of FSHD is the aberrant expression of the DUX4 gene, which encodes a transcription factor that activates a cascade of hundreds of typically silent target genes. The DUX4 transcription factor comprises two main parts: the DNA-binding domain (DBD) and transcriptional activation domain (TAD), which is responsible for activating downstream target genes. Our approach is centered on overexpressing a modified form of the DUX4-DBD lacking the TAD. DUX4-DBD competes for DUX4 binding sites, inhibiting pathogenic DUX4 and stopping downstream gene activation. We are also modulating the components of our engineered protein, exploring the use of fusing a KRAB (Krüppel Associated Box) repressor domain to maximize our therapeutic potential as a suppressor of DUX4-activated genes.
igem_Michigan_2024: 1,4-Dioxane is a Group 2B carcinogen that poses immediate risk to human health and is a byproduct of many common industrial processes. For over two decades, 1,4-dioxane was improperly disposed of into a tributary that feeds into the Huron River, the primary water supply for the city of Ann Arbor, Michigan. The current remediation method is expensive and inefficient. Additionally, it introduces bromate, another carcinogen, to the water in the process. Our team engineered and optimized a freshwater bacteria (Pseudomonas putida S16) with a tetrahydrofuran monooxygenase gene complex (THFMO) known to naturally degrade 1,4-dioxane. Our bacteria are suited to operate within a bioreactor, which we aim to implement in tandem with existing infrastructure. Our ultimate goal is to improve the sustainability, efficiency, and efficacy of the current water treatment process.
igem_Outaouais_2024: Our team consists of 50 passionate mentors and students from three academic institutions in Gatineau, Québec, Canada. In our inaugural iGEM season, we have focused our efforts on tackling plastic pollution and the climate crisis, exploring how to position our project and outreach activities to maximize our impact on these urgent environmental issues. Our project, TIME2ACT, leverages PET-degrading enzymes to transform poorly recycled PET plastic waste into durable and high-performance mesoporous materials, with applications in carbon capture and electrochemical storage and conversion industries. By utilizing our newly acquired skills in synthetic biology, entrepreneurship, and communication, we strive to give new value to the plastic debris that pollutes our forests, lakes, and rivers, while also contributing to global efforts to combat climate change and raise awareness in our community that it is indeed TIME2ACT.
igem_Duke_2024: CAR-T cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable success in treating blood-based cancers, but faces significant challenges in combating solid tumors. ATLAS (Antigen Triggered Ligand Amplification System) is a genetic circuit designed to enhance the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy in difficult cancers. The system addresses antigen loss, a major challenge where tumors reduce or lose expression of target antigens, that limits CAR-T efficacy. ATLAS combines two synthetic receptors, low-affinity CAR and high-affinity synNotch, to amplify antigen availability at the tumor site. Upon synNotch activation by tumor-specific ligands, the system secretes soluble antigens that stimulate nearby CAR-T cells, creating an activation feedback loop. This process recruits immune cells to the tumor through cytokine release, enhancing the immune response in tumors with diminished antigen expression. By increasing the local concentration of antigens, ATLAS aims to improve CAR-T persistence and effectiveness to treat solid tumors.
igem_USAFA_2024: The USAFA iGEM 2024 team is focused on optimizing biosilicification by expressing the INP-silicatein-α gene in E. coli to address global and local environmental challenges, such as CO2 production in the cement industry, desertification, and agricultural topsoil degradation. Our efforts are divided into three key areas: dust mitigation, plant growth in biosilicified soil, and cement brick formation. We verified that SiO2 formation is catalyzed by our new part. We were able to eliminate the use of urea in biocementation and our biosilicification produced less ammonium than microbially induced calcite precipitation while allowing plant germination in biocemented soil.  Throughout the project, our team engaged with the community by participating in local science events, consulting with farmers, and receiving insights from a rotorcraft mechanic. Our work has contributed valuable research to genetic engineering and sustainable development.
igem_SHSD_2024: In modern society, PET plastic plays an increasingly significant role in our daily lives. Correspondingly, the challenge of effectively degrading PET plastics has drawn the attention of researchers and environmentalists, among other people who concern about the environment. Building on previous research, we created a new silkworm strain by microinjecting recombinant gene expression vectors containing the Fast-PETase and MHETase enzymes, which have been proven to facilitate the degradation of PET plastics. Through further experiments, we demonstrated that the transgenic cocoons secreted by these genetically modified silkworms could effectively degrade PET plastic products. This outcome provides a new solution for biodegradation of PET plastics. Our long-term goal is to achieve industrial-scale production of this new transgenic silk and promote sustainability by enabling the recycling of PET plastics through their degradation byproducts, such as TPA, MHET, and EG, as they are also the raw materials of PET plastics.
igem_HongKong-UCCKE_2024: Ningxia, China, faces significant agricultural challenges due to high evaporation rates, resulting in crop failures. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach utilizing genetically engineered E. coli to produce hyaluronic acid hydrogels. Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring polymer known for its exceptional water-retention properties. By applying hyaluronic acid into the agricultural sector, we aim to create a cost-effective and sustainable solution to combat drought-induced crop losses. Our strategy involves genetically modifying E. coli to express enzymes that are crucial in producing hyaluronic acid. The modified bacteria will produce hyaluronic acid, which can be extracted and used to create hydrogels. These hydrogels will be designed to absorb and retain moisture in the soil, reducing water loss and improving soil hydration levels. The ultimate goal of this project is to assist farmers in drought-prone regions, such as Ningxia, with a practical and affordable tool to enhance crop yields.
igem_Missouri-Miners_2024: Craspase, an RNA-activated protease, integrates a Cas enzyme (gRAMP) and the Csx29 protease to target specific proteins upon RNA binding. This project explores utilizing Craspase, delivered via lambda bacteriophages, to neutralize antibiotic resistance genes in bacteria, particularly ampicillin resistance. Specifically, we will employ an engineered fusion protein to modulate Runella bacterial gasdermin protein, inducing cell death through pyroptosis in response to mRNA indicative of ampicillin resistance. With the rising threat of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, innovative approaches such as bacteriophage therapy are crucial. Our strategy involves modifying a plasmid to express both the Craspase system and the fusion protein anchoring the gasdermin, which will be introduced into ampicillin-resistant E. coli. We aim to monitor bacterial responses on agar plates supplemented with ampicillin. This work aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of phage-mediated delivery of Craspase and fusion proteins in targeting antibiotic resistance, offering a novel approach to combat multidrug-resistant infections and enhance medicine.
igem_NYC-Empire-State_2024: As of 2023, over 6.5 million people in the United States alone suffer from chronic wounds. This means that annually, around 40 million people deal with painful, slow healing or recurring wounds that are expensive to treat. With Hydrolink, we aim to engineer Lactobacillus reuteri to be able to detect staph. aureus, the most common wound pathogen, and respond by secreting targeted antimicrobial proteins. This detection is achieved with autoinducing peptide (AIP), which is used by staph. aureus for quorum sensing. After achieving successful transformation, the bacteria can be integrated into a hydrogel material to form a living wound dressing. This method has advantages over alternatives like traditional wound dressings, which must be taken off to check for infection, causing pain and inefficiency. In addition to our wet-lab research, we performed computational modeling and developed a fluorometer to be used with the hydrogel product.
igem_NPU-CHINA_2024: Modern global warming has posed serious threat to climate and related life on earth. The greenhouse gas emissions caused by fossil fuels are the main culprit of global warming. It is of great urgent to develop renewable and green energy to solve this issue. Lignocellulose biomass is promising precusor for developing renewable energy to cope with greenhouse gas emissions. However, the current lignocellulose degradation methods are limited by low efficiency and are environmentally unfriendly and energy consuming. What can be done with synthetic biology? In this project, we engineered the tgenes of cytochrome C mature protein (Ccm) operon and transformed into P. putida, creating a cellular factory that produce abundant ligninolytic enzymes, which simutaneously produce manganese oxide acting as ligninolytic nanozyme. Finally, the enzymes plus nanozyme sucessfully realize lignin degradation with high efficiency.
igem_Hangzhou-SDG_2024: Heavy metals pose serious health risks, including neurotoxicity, kidney damage, and cancer. Our team enhances bioremediation by engineering E. coli to express rice metallothionein (OsMTI-1b) for effective metal binding and genes from Sporosarcina pasteurii for Microbiologically Induced Calcite Precipitation, turning heavy metal ions into easily removable precipitates. Our engineered bacteria are designed for use in facilities or regions requiring heavy metal remediation, such as industrial wastewater treatment plants. This approach ensures that the solution is practical and scalable, providing a greener alternative to conventional methods and contributing to safer water supplies worldwide.
igem_Nanjing-BioX_2024: Faced with the problem of diabetes, which is skyrocketing globally due to excessive intake of sucrose, we would like to use a natural sugar substitute, allose, as a healthier alternative to sucrose. However, the cost of natural extraction and production methods for allose remains high, and to address this challenge, our team developed an allose biosensor based on alsR transcriptional regulators. The sensor has been rigorously tested and demonstrated specificity and high efficiency to convert allose production into a real-time fluorescence response. Meanwhile, we have further optimized the sensor performance by using computational prediction and molecular docking techniques, combined with random mutagenesis, which lays a solid foundation for achieving low-cost and large-scale microbial synthesis of allose.
igem_Shanghai-BioX_2024: The incidence of myocarditis has increased after COVID-19, posing a threat to public health. Traditional Chinese medicine, Salvia miltiorrhiza (Danshen), its active compounds, such as tanshinone, and a similar structure diterpenoid carnosic acid, which is also extracted from Salvia, have proven effective in treating cardiovascular diseases, including anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective benefits. However, traditional production methods are limited by high cost and time-consuming. To address this issue, we use Saccharomyces cerevisiae, leveraging its inherent MVA pathway to construct a novel synthetic pathway for the efficient production of tanshinone and carnosic acid. This sustainable, scalable method may revolutionize cardiovascular drug production, expanding applications in drug development and combating cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases.
igem_Hangzhou-BioX_2024: The huge aquaculture industry in China faces serious threats from Aeromonas hydrophila, a pathogenic bacterium that can cause motile septicemia in aquatic animals. This pathogen utilizes AHL molecules to activate quorum sensing and express virulence factors. To combat A. hydrophila, we introduced AHL lactonases from various bacteria to Bacillus subtilis. By degrading AHL, our engineered B. subtilis can reduce the virulence of A. hydrophila and protect aquaculture animals. In the future, we hope that this approach could be scaled up for widespread application, potentially integrating with existing aquaculture practices to provide a sustainable and effective solution against bacterial pathogens.
igem_JLU-China_2024: Our project focuses on developing an optimized near-infrared II (NIR-II) imaging probe using a recombinant human serum albumin (rHSA) mutant. By mutating the cysteine residue at position 476 to glycine (C476G), we successfully disrupted the disulfide bond between Cys476 and Cys487, exposing a reactive thiol group. This modification significantly enhances the covalent binding efficiency between rHSA and NIR-II dyes, particularly the Cn-1080 family (such as CO-1080). Our research includes computational simulations and experimental validation, demonstrating improved binding affinity, stability, and imaging performance in deep tissues, such as the blood-testis and blood-brain barriers. The probe simplifies preparation under mild conditions and has broad applications in biomedical imaging, tumor surgery navigation, and diagnostics. This novel approach offers a robust and reproducible solution for advancing NIR-II imaging in complex biological environments.
igem_NMU-China_2024: Today, humanity is confronted with numerous challenges, which makes space exploration increasingly urgent. Nevertheless, the current astronaut suits have deficiencies in guaranteeing the safety and long-term survival of astronauts. Inspired by this, our team has designed an integrated Luminescent Rescue Life Support System by applying the principles of synthetic biology. The LuminAid in the project is a photosynthetic autotrophic fluorescent life-saving device, applicable to both marine and space scenarios. In the marine context, it is a collapsible bag containing engineered bacterial powder, which proliferates and glows when encountering seawater, enhancing the visibility of the person in distress. In the space setting, the symbiotic system of algae and bacteria enables the astronaut suit to emit light for illumination and orientation, and it can also produce oxygen and organic substances to supply the life activities of astronauts and meet emergency demands. The project is widely applicable and innovative.
igem_CHINA-HUBU-WUHAN_2024: In the contemporary world, chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, and colitis are progressively emerging as significant global health threats.  The engineering strain chosen for our project is Zymomonas mobilis, primarily due to its anaerobic fermentation capability and high tolerance towards sugar and acid. This strain exhibits enhanced suitability for the intestinal environment and produces fructooligosaccharides, which can effectively promote the growth of gut microbiota and potentially achieve targeted colonization. By employing targeted metabolic engineering design, modification, testing, and application of Zymomonas mobilis, we aim to develop a synbiotic microbial therapy that integrates prevention, diagnostic reporting, and responsive treatment modules. Compared to conventional treatment methods, synbiotic therapy offers superior levels of safety, stability, adaptability, and targeting. Moreover, the duration of its medicinal effects is prolonged, effectively addressing the requirement for patients to adhere to specific timing and dosages in traditional treatments.
igem_Bioplus-China_2024: This project is committed to developing an innovative aromatic product aimed at relieving stress. Our core ingredient is β-ionone, a fragrant molecule found in a variety of flowers, which has been demonstrated to have significant sedative and mood-soothing effects. Through synthetic biology techniques, we have genetically modified Escherichia coli to express Osmanthus fragrans carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 4 (OfCCD4), an enzyme that can convert carotenoids into β-ionone. To achieve sustainable development, our project has adopted an innovative method: using discarded tea leaves or tea dregs, which are rich in carotenoids, as substrates for the synthesis of β-ionone. Our final detection experiment successfully verified the synthesis of β-ionone through gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis. Our project not only focuses on the functionality of the product but also emphasizes a design philosophy that values health, fashion, and environmental sustainability.
igem_Lund_2024: Cattle release around 80 million tons of methane into the atmosphere annually, significantly contributing to global warming. The methane is produced by methanogens in the cow’s rumen as a by-product of enteric fermentation, also resulting in energy loss for the animal. We aim to reduce the methane emissions from cattle by synthetically engineering Cupriavidus necator to produce bromoform, a known methanogenesis inhibitor. The engineered bacteria would ideally colonize the rumen and become a permanent member of the microbiome, continuously inhibiting methane production from within. Our gene insert consists of a bromoperoxidase gene originating from marine bromoform-producing organisms, as well as a hydrogen peroxidase gene to supply the required substrate for bromoperoxidase. While we successfully transformed our simplest construct, only one bromoperoxidase showed protein expression. However, in-vitro co-culturing of C. Necator with methanogens showed decreased methane production, probably due to its competition for the same resources as methanogens.
igem_Bioplus-Shanghai_2024: Danshen, the root of Salvia miltiorrhiza, is widely recognized as an effective medicine for treating cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, but there are many limitations in the extraction of its active components. To overcome these limitations, our project employs synthetic biology techniques to design two synthetic pathways. Utilizing endogenously produced 4-coumaroyl-CoA in tobacco as the acyl donor, we introduce key enzymes and precursor substances exogenously to synthesize rosmarinic acid. In pathway one, we introduce danshensu, SmRAS10, and SmCYP98A14; in pathway two, we introduce 4-hydroxyphenyllactate, SmRAS10, SmCYP98A14, and SmCYP98A75. LC-MS/MS results indicate that both pathways are capable of synthesizing rosmarinic acid in tobacco leaves. Moving forward, the project will focus on further optimizing production efficiency.
