We established TriScale, a hierarchical in silico pipeline integrating signal peptide–linker–based peroxisomal targeting design, rational tHMGR enzyme engineering, and system-level growth modeling for predictive and knowledge-guided prototyping. Building on this framework, we developed a compartmentalized metabolism strategy, relocating the entire MVA pathway into peroxisomes to enhance flux and isolate toxic intermediates. To bridge lab design with application, we created the low-cost, automated Integrated Fermentation & Processing System (iFPS), streamlining production from inoculation to crude lysate collection. Our integrated approach demonstrates a sustainable, economically viable route to convert pollutants into valuable cosmetic ingredients，while contributing innovations in culture analysis and fermentation processing.
igem_OUC-China_2025: In response to growing climate concerns, biological CO2 capture and utilization technologies have attracted significant attention. Beyond direct CO2 fixation, the biological assimilation of the liquid one-carbon compounds, such as methanol, offers a promising alternative route for converting CO2 into value-added products. Aureobasidium melanogenum, a kind of poly-extremotolerant yeast-like fungus, exhibits remarkable potential for producing diverse bioproducts. Here, we established a CRISPR‑Cas9 gene‑editing system for A. melanogenum and elucidated the mechanisms underlying its methanol metabolism. By reprogramming key metabolic pathways, we constructed an engineered strain capable of synthesizing glucose from methanol. Furthermore, to optimize the cultivation of A. melanogenum, we developed a real-time methanol monitoring and automatic feeding device based on a gas-liquid exchange model, enabling convenient and accurate methanol concentration measurement. This study provides a foundational framework for leveraging A. melanogenumin the bioconversion of C1 compounds toward chemical production, highlighting its potential for sustainable carbon utilization.
igem_Rochester_2025: Since the Mariner 4 flyby, Mars has inspired interplanetary exploration, but high payload costs limit human settlement. Our team proposes PHAntom, a synthetic biology system using engineered E. coli to convert Martian CO₂ into bioplastics and metabolites. Our two-strain E. coli system converts CO₂ into PHBV via an acetate intermediate. Strain 1 autotrophically fixes CO₂ and secretes acetate using the pta–ackA pathway. Strain 2, aided by tdcB/tdcE for propionyl-CoA supply and tesB/yciA to balance 3HB/3HV monomers, converts acetate into PHBV. A bicarbonate-responsive cAMP–CRP mechanism enhances transcription under high HCO₃⁻, while CRISPRi knockdown of gltA diverts acetyl-CoA from the TCA cycle, optimizing acetate production and PHBV yield. Team PHAntom has built a clinostat to simulate non-Earth gravity conditions and an extrusion system to convert PHBV granules into printable filaments. PHAntom enables sustainable off-world biomaterial production through integrated carbon capture, adaptive metabolism, and on-site manufacturing
igem_Waterloo_2025: Catheter associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) are the most common hospital infection, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations such as those in long-term care homes or the critically ill. While the standard treatments for these infections rely primarily on antibiotics, the increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistant infections demands for an alternative solution. To combat this issue, we have developed HydroGuard, a biocompatible, infection-responsive hydrogel with controlled phage release. Our hydrogel, made up of gelatin methacryloyl, degrades in the presence of gelatinase (gelE), a protein naturally produced by E.faecalis during infection. The degradation of gelatin in the hydrogel releases the embedded phage cocktail, which targets and eradicates the biofilm. Using a combined wet-lab and computational approach, our work demonstrates the viability of this solution by incorporating the gelE gene into E.coli for lab-safe proof of concept solution.
igem_HKUST-GZ_2025: Lychee deteriorates rapidly after harvest due to high respiration, browning, and fungal decay. Current preservation methods rely on costly cold chains and chemical additives. Our project proposes a sustainable synthetic biology solution integrating melatonin biosynthesis and bioengineered wax coating. Engineered Bacillus subtilis produces melatonin to reduce respiration, delay browning, and enhance lychee immunity. Meanwhile, a LacI–lactose regulatory system promotes fatty acid accumulation, enabling the formation of a protective wax layer that retains moisture and prevents microbial invasion. Complemented by AI-assisted dry-lab tools—BactaGenome for bacterial genome analysis, SynbioMCP for intuitive biological design, and a drone-based spraying system for large-scale application—our approach provides an eco-friendly and intelligent lychee preservation platform that extends shelf life and reduces postharvest waste.
igem_BUAP-Puebla_2025: Premature newborns often face respiratory distress due to underdeveloped lungs, requiring pulmonary surfactant for survival. Current treatments are costly, rely on animal-derived sources, and remain inaccesible to many healthcare systems wolrdwide. Our project uses synthetic biology and biomanufacturing to create an alternative surfactant that is animal-free, affordable, and scalable. By engineering microorganisms to produce key surfactant proteins, we aim to deliver a sustainable solution that bridges health inequities and reduces dependence on traditional animal-derived products. This approach not only addresses a pressing medical challenge but also introduces an ethical and environmentally responsible production pipeline. Through our work, we envision a future where every premature infant, regardless of geography or economic status, can access life-saving pulmonary surfactant demonstrating how synthetic biology can transform global health challenges into opportunities for innovation, sustainability, and equity.
igem_SUSTechOCEAN_2025: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) pose severe threats to marine ecosystems, aquaculture, and human health. Traditional control methods are often inefficient, environmentally risky, and prone to secondary pollution. To address these challenges, the SUSTechOCEAN team developed an intelligent and controllable HAB mitigation system that integrates artificial intelligence prediction with synthetic biology intervention. Using a deep learning–based OI-SwinUnet model, we predict the risk of HAB occurrence from environmental parameters such as nutrient concentrations, temperature, and dissolved oxygen. When the predicted risk exceeds a defined threshold, engineered Bacillus subtilis expresses Surfactin C14—a biodegradable, low-toxicity biosurfactant with strong algicidal activity—under blue-light induction. Meanwhile, red light activates the expression of the phage-derived YonE protein, which depletes intracellular NAD⁺ and triggers cell death, ensuring biosafety. This system achieves intelligent linkage between “prediction” and “intervention,” providing a sustainable, eco-friendly, and safe synthetic biology solution for marine ecosystem protection.
igem_HUBU-China_2025: By integrating enzyme engineering with synthetic biology, we have developed a highly efficient and specific biodegradation platform with exceptional potential. Starting from ADH3—the most active OTA hydrolase reported to date—we rationally designed the S88E mutant, whose additional hydrogen-bond network increases catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) by 3.7-fold. To surmount the remaining catalytic bottleneck, we mined the sequence space of ADH3 and identified the homologous enzyme LIADH (73 % identity) that possesses twice the native activity of ADH3. Structure-guided redesign of LIADH yielded the I326A variant; removal of the γ-branched side chain relieves steric congestion at the acyl-enzyme intermediate, affording a further 75 % improvement in activity. Collectively, we obtained two high-performance biocatalysts—ADH3-S88E and LIADH-I326A—and accomplished the first comprehensive structural, kinetic, and mechanistic characterization of any OTA hydrolase.
igem_XJTLU-CHINA_2025: Green tides caused by Ulva prolifera have become a seasonal ecological disaster in Qingdao. The traditional physical salvage methods are time-consuming and laborious. So our team’s project uses a synthetic biology solution to address green tides at the source—spores, a key driver of bloom recurrence.​ Since the core of our project is "capture spore", we rearranged letters and named our project “O! Super Carpet”. It is composed of three main modules. We would like to name them after spells from Harry Potter. First, the 'Ennervate' survival spell ensures that our engineered bacteria can survive in high-salinity seawater. Second, the 'Permanent Sticking' functional spell is responsible for efficiently capturing Ulva spores with specificity. Finally, the 'Avada Kedavra' biosafety spell guarantees safety of the project in open environments.  By combining synthetic biology with ecological insight, our project aims to demonstrate how engineered microbes can offer sustainable solutions to marine environmental crises.
igem_XJTLU-Software_2025: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are essential natural molecules with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity. To accelerate AMP discovery, we developed SPADE, a Systematic Platform for Antimicrobial peptide Database with Evaluation, integrating and standardizing data from four major AMP repositories (APD3, DRAMP, DBAASP, and LAMP), resulting in over 39,000 curated peptides. After rigorous cleaning and unification of experimental conditions, we established the AMP-Oriented Six tasks (AMPOS) dataset and the AMP-Oriented Multi-Property Prediction Task (AMPPT), covering classification and regression subtasks including MIC, half-life, and hemolytic activity. We further designed the AMP-Oriented Multi-task Model (AOMM), achieving state-of-the-art performance across all AMPPT subtasks. Additionally, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system was implemented to enhance intelligent AMP searching. Overall, SPADE provides an integrated, reproducible, and extensible foundation for AMP data analysis, model benchmarking, and AI-assisted peptide design in modern bioinformatics.
igem_XJTLU-AI-China_2025: Plastic pollution represents a growing global crisis, while biodegrading enzymes provide a sustainable route to plastic recycling. To accelerate enzyme identification, Plaszyme integrates AI-based models that learn from both biological and chemical representations to predict enzyme–polymer interactions with interpretability and precision. Our framework combines machine learning classifiers and structure-aware dual-tower neural networks, enabling multi-level prediction from amino acid sequences to 3D enzyme–polymer compatibility. A lightweight Web App offers browser-based batch prediction, visualization, and interpretability without local setup. In parallel, we curated and released PlaszymeDB, an open-access database compiling verified enzyme–plastic pairs, sequences, structures, and physicochemical descriptors under FAIR principles. Through continued development and open dissemination via iGEM and the Web App, Plaszyme establishes a unified resource for data-driven exploration of plastic biodegradation and sustainable material recycling.
igem_NENU-China_2025: Lactose intolerance, a prevalent global condition, causes symptoms like diarrhea and abdominal pain due to lactase deficiency in the gut. Current dietary management lacks long-term efficacy and impacts life quality. We propose a sustainable synthetic biology-based therapy using engineered Bifidobacterium. This strain is modified with a optimized bgaB lactase and LacY lactose transporter for efficient lactose metabolism. It also incorporates a genetic circuit with a deoxycholic acid-inducible MucBP adhesion protein and an AI-2/CcdB-mediated population control system. This design enables stable colonization at an appropriate density, ensuring continuous lactose breakdown for long-term management of lactose intolerance.
igem_RUBochum_2025: Desferrioxamine is the most economically important siderophore, used in life-saving chelation therapy for thalassemia patients and iron overload disorders, plus industrial applications like gallium recovery from wastewater. However, high production costs limit its accessibility. Current production relies on Streptomyces pilosus, which suffers from slow growth, low yields, and complex lifecycles that complicate industrial-scale fermentation, making it unsuitable as a production platform. Our team is transferring the desferrioxamine biosynthetic gene cluster to Rhodococcus, which doesn't naturally produce desferrioxamine but is well-established in industry for producing complex secondary metabolites. Rhodococcus offers fast growth, high scalability, and excellent fermentation characteristics. Both species belong to Actinobacteria, sharing similar genetic architecture, codon usage, and metabolic frameworks necessary for expressing the desferrioxamine pathway. To confirm successful pathway integration and transcriptional activity during transfer, we designed a split-GFP monitoring system. We aim to reduce desferrioxamine production costs and increase its accessibility for medical and industrial applications.
igem_Austin-UTexas_2025: Rapid growth of algae in response to environmental pressures, such as climate change, has increased cyanotoxin prevalence in freshwater ecosystems, exceeding safety standards. The most prevalent cyanotoxins produced are microcystins, known to cause harm to humans and animals upon ingestion. Current methods of identifying microcystins involve complex and expensive quantitative assays, which are impractical for field deployment. Our team explored a method to safely detect and degrade these toxins by engineering Acinetobacter baylyi (ADP1) to perform as a biosensor and biodegrader. The system detects environmental DNA (eDNA) released by microcystin-producing cyanobacteria. Upon detection of a target region of DNA within the microcystin gene pathway, the biosensor will activate genes responsible for enzymatic microcystin degradation, providing a potential strategy for eliminating microcystins.
igem_UMaryland_2025: RGBio focused on creating an “optogenetic toolkit” allowing regulation of three genes or regulons using red, green, and blue light. This toolkit uses three optogenetic switches to orthogonally regulate gene expression in response to each type of light stimulus. Our team applied this toolkit to bioplastic synthesis and modulation of polymer properties. Bioplastics can be made from standard carbon sources or from waste carbon, making the system robust and allowing for remediation of molecules like waste acetate that are produced in large amounts yearly. Other teams and researchers can use our optogenetic toolkit to regulate their genes of interest without the need for induction molecules, and can easily remove or replace components of our optogenetic switches through a simple restriction digest and Gibson Assembly-compatible insert.
igem_Aachen_2025: With our project NCLOSE, we are tackling the growing global challenge of nitrate pollution. Agriculture is one of the main drivers: synthetic fertilizers and animal manure release large amounts of ammonium, which soil microbes convert to nitrate. NCLOSE aims to counteract this by producing γ-polyglutamic acid (PGA), a natural polymer capable of reversibly binding ammonium, directly in manure. This reduces nitrate leaching while providing crops with a slow-release nutrient source.  We introduced three genes encoding PGA synthetase into Clostridium cellulovorans, an anaerobic, cellulolytic bacterium, well-equipped for growth in manure. Additionally, we created resources to make this chassis more accessible for future teams, including adapted workflows, a genome-scale model and a taxonomic analysis. The development of a solid biosafety concept was also a central aspect. Through integrated human practices, we ensured NCLOSE remains safe, sustainable and socially responsible, turning manure from part of the problem into part of the solution.
igem_SZU-China_2025: As the world's largest citrus producer, China contributes one-quarter of global citrus output, yet faces severe threats from the concealed brown citrus aphid. To address this, we present APHiGO—an RNAi-based platform for sustainable aphid control, integrating smart monitoring with precise molecular intervention. APHiGO’s early-warning module uses engineered Bacillus subtilis to detect honeydew and emit volatile signals, monitored via IoT sensors. Upon detection, RNAi molecules targeting vital aphid genes are delivered via trunk injection. Packaged in engineered virus-like particles, these molecules are efficiently ingested, silencing key genes and impeding development. For localized outbreaks, modified Metarhizium fungi deliver dsRNA externally and internally, enhancing lethality and delaying resistance. By combining biosensing, RNAi targeting, and biocontrol, APHiGO transitions pest management from chemical reliance to intelligent, sustainable precision agriculture.
igem_Tsinghua-A_2025: Protein translation proceeds discontinuously, with ribosomes pausing to enable co-translational folding of nascent chains. Although ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) has revealed widespread translational pauses, existing mRNA design frameworks largely ignore these kinetic features. Here, we identify conserved pausing sites across multiple human cell lines using EIF-based Ribo-seq and propose that such pauses facilitate proper protein folding. We developed PACD (Pause-Aware Codon Design), a computational framework that incorporates ribosome pausing information into mRNA optimization. A neural model trained on pausing sequences enables predictive integration with LinearDesign to preserve beneficial pauses during codon optimization. While pause-constrained designs slightly reduce mRNA stability and CAI, they are expected to enhance folding efficiency. This study represents the first systematic attempt to link translational pausing with codon design, providing a foundation for engineering “pause-aware” synthetic genes with improved structural fidelity.
igem_EPFL_2025: Wildfires present major global challenges, from CO2 emissions and ecosystem destruction to severe public health impacts. Current firefighting methods also carry significant drawbacks. Pyronix offers a new approach, harnessing synthetic biology to create a more sustainable solution. We engineered a hydrogel-based fire retardant assembled from components produced by microorganisms. The gel structure is composed of cellulose and chitosan. Silica nanoparticles and a fire-retardant protein are embedded in the gel to improve its fire resistance. To deploy the hydrogel, we developed an artificial intelligence equipped drone for safe and automated firefighting, supporting life-saving decisions made by the operators.  We engineered yeast strains for enhanced chitosan production, bacterial cells building up silica nanoparticles, and expression systems to produce fire retardant proteins. We assembled the components into a gel-like structure to study its fire-retardant properties. Pyronix provides a solid foundation for developing sustainable firefighting methods from production to deployment.
igem_Leiden_2025: The lack of precise control over post-translational modifications in synthetic protein production is a significant obstacle in research and biomanufacturing, especially in the development of biopharmaceuticals. To overcome this we developed Self Integrating Scaffolds (SIS), protein fragments flanked by split inteins. This project aims to insert a glycosylated SIS in Immunoglobuline G. To optimise our SIS, it’s necessary to test how efficient two pairs of inteins can be used together. Because of that, we have designed a FRET assay, which enables us to test split intein pairs in high-throughput for their quantitative kinetic compatibility in real-time using only a plate reader. In addition, we applied dynamical modelling, docking simulations, structural comparisons, mathematical modelling and programming in R-studio to provide a more in-depth understanding of all these aspects regarding our SIS and FRET assay. Together, our results lay the foundation of using split inteins to change the world of protein engineering.
igem_SPC_2025: To alleviate the problem of plastic pollution and mitigate the serious impacts made by plastic on our environment, our team worked on multiple DNA combinations to break down PET. Our solution is HotPETase, an enzyme that can degrade PET plastics readily at high temperatures. We have paired it up with the genes BaCBM2 and CsgA respectively, then combined all three genes together to form our final gene combination. Out of all gene constructs, HotPETase-BaCBM2 showed the best performance, having the greatest increase in absorbance and the largest decrease in mass of the PET fragment at 70°C. Our main target gene combination, CsgA-HotPETase-BaCBM2 showed promising results during the absorbance test, having the second highest increase in absorbance at 60°C. SEM imaging was conducted on the PET samples, with irregular cracks being observed on the PET surface, in contrast to the smooth surface of the control.
igem_Concordia-Shanghai_2025: In response to the global challenge of plastic waste, our iGEM project aims to develop innovative biological pathways for the upcycling of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic into high-value products, such as BHB (Beta Hydroxybutyrate).  Our approach designs synthetic pathways in E. coli and P. putida, enabling them to convert PET waste into Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) and later BHB. Utilizing computational tools and Flux Balance Analysis (FBA), we will optimize the engineered pathways to enhance the flux towards PHB production. This will include the use of kinetic models to predict and refine enzyme activity based on varying substrate concentrations. By designing and constructing novel biological parts, we aim to establish an innovative production pathway that aligns with circular economy principles. This will not only facilitate the conversion of PET plastic waste into valuable products but also provide a sustainable solution to a pressing environmental issue.
igem_FHS-NB-ZJ-China_2025: Peach gummosis seriously harms peach tree health, mainly triggered by fungal infections and environmental stress. It causes bark cracking and gummy exudation, weakening trees severely or even killing them. Current controls depend on chemicals and agricultural management, but problems like drug resistance and pollution remain, leaving a gap for efficient, eco-friendly solutions.  ‘GumEraser+’ proposes to manipulate three key factors required for disease occurrence:  1) Apply specific RNA-based biopesticides to inhibit the activity of pathogens;  2) Promote the cultivation of disease-resistant host varieties;  3) Promote pruning of peach trees to improve orchard air circulation.  The ‘+’ symbol here stands for three aspirations in addressing it: 1) Boost farmers’ income; 2) Enhance personal growth; 3) Promote knowledge transfer.
igem_Taipei-KCISLK-V3_2025: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of global mortality, highlighting the need for rapid and sensitive diagnostic technologies. We developed an integrated nucleic acid–based biosensing platform that detects CVD-related microRNAs (miRNAs) with high specificity. The biosensor combines three-way junction (3WJ) probe recognition and a split G-quadruplex (G4) DNAzyme switch, where target-induced linker release reconstitutes the G4 structure. The G4/hemin complex catalyzes the oxidation of TMB, producing measurable electrochemical signals on a portable reader. The system achieved a limit of detection of 480 pM, demonstrating strong sensitivity and specificity. To accelerate probe optimization, machine learning (ML) models trained on experimental datasets (2500 miRNA-specific 3WJ probes and 728 split G4 probes) reached 83% accuracy for the 3WJ model and 80% for the split G4 model. This data-driven biosensor framework bridges biosensing probe design and ML prediction, enabling rapid, customizable, and cost-effective miRNA diagnostics for cardiovascular and other diseases.
igem_HongKong-HS_2025: Significance Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most ubiquitous types of cancer in Hong Kong, with approximately 10,000 new cases diagnosed annually. Early detection can significantly improve prognosis, with successful treatment rates exceeding 90%. However, the current mainstream screening methods, such as colonoscopy, FOBT, and FIT, have their limitations of being invasive and inconvenient. Project Mechanics Our project aims to create a tool that detects CRC in its early stages. Our ColoTrace kit detects overexpressed microRNAs (miR) of CRC in the faecal samples, and create coloured proteins that indicate a positive detection. Engineering and Results Six toehold switches that detect miR-92a-3p and miR-135b-5p are designed, and one of the ligated toehold-plasmids was successfully cloned in E. coli, and two of the toehold-plasmids showed strong expression when triggered by the target microRNA.
igem_Institut-Le-Rosey-CH_2025: The project aims to develop a low-cost, rapid, and user-friendly diagnostic kit for detecting EGFR mutations in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), which are associated with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The system integrates Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) with CRISPR-Cas9 amplicon cleavage and a Lateral Flow Assay (LFA) readout, enabling a one-pot, isothermal assay that delivers a visual result without specialized equipment. This approach aims to make early molecular screening for NSCLC accessible, especially in resource-limited regions.
igem_City-of-London-UK_2025: One of the most neglected tropical diseases, Cryptosporidiosis kills an estimated 200,000 children every year and 10 million disability adjusted life years lost annually. It is caused by a parasite, and spreads through infected water samples globally. Current methods, such as qPCR, are expensive, unreliable and affected by inhibitors in faecal samples, with the most common methods having a sensitivity of around 40-60%.    Using Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification, we designed a novel point of care diagnostic for the 18s rRNA of Cryptosporidium, designing an efficient primer set, and four new fusion Bst polymerases, with subdomains designed to increase reverse transcriptase activity, thermostability and inhibitor tolerance. Targeting 18s rRNA allows the test to detect 1 oocyst/gram of faecal sample (compared to qPCR’s 300/gram). Results are shown colourimetrically for easy use. With our model and education work, we made the test even more accessible.    It's time to shine a LAMP On Cryptosporidiosis!
igem_UNILausanne_2025: Rare earth elements (REEs) and tellurium are essential for high-tech and renewable technologies, yet less than 1% are currently recycled. To address this, we developed a sustainable, bio-based strategy to recover these elements from e-waste streams. We engineered a modular system using amyloid protein fibers displaying REE-binding proteins, achieving high-affinity capture of REE ions and creating a powerful part collection. Mathematical modeling and molecular dynamics simulations guided design optimization, while a business plan and market analysis evaluated commercial viability. For tellurium recovery, we harnessed the Ter operon to efficiently reduce toxic tellurite into elemental tellurium. To promote our project and raise awareness of synthetic biology, we conducted extensive outreach through exhibitions, workshops, educational activities, blogs, podcasts, and interactive games across hospitals, museums, and schools. Thus, our project demonstrates an integrated synthetic biology platform for the biological recovery of REEs and tellurium from electronic waste.
igem_Mingdao_2025: Through IHP, we identified two key challenges from stakeholders’ perspectives: insufficient efficiency of PLA-degrading enzymes and unclear recycling classification. To address the first issue, we engineered recombinant enzymes (AC, CA, DP, PK) and developed an auto-induction measurement system for high-throughput screening, with PK variants showing the most promising activity. For the second issue, we aligned with the SDGs by organizing a target field to test PLA usage in isolation and submitting a citizen proposal to advocate for clearer waste management policies and the establishment of industrial composting facilities in Taiwan, providing a practical solution to misclassification. Our project demonstrates the integration of enzyme engineering with community engagement to advance PLA degradation and sustainable waste management.
igem_BNDS-China_2025: Cats are among the most popular companion animals worldwide, yet many of their health issues remain undiagnosed due to subtle symptoms and limited diagnostic tools. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), often aggravated by hairball accumulation, is a prevalent chronic condition that compromises digestive health. To address this, we developed MeowTrack, a programmable therapeutic probiotic platform that detects, treats, and records feline gut health. The system senses taurocholic acid (food intake) and calprotectin (IBD biomarker) and integrates these inputs through an AND logic gate, ensuring responses occur only under disease conditions with food available. Upon activation, MeowTrack expresses keratin-degrading enzymes to remove hairballs, butyrate-producing enzymes to restore gut balance, and chromoproteins or fluorescent proteins to visualize disease states in feces. Additionally, a Retro-Cascorder module records transcriptional events linked to inflammation, while a smart litter box equipped with fluorescence detection enables seamless, at-home monitoring of feline gut health.
igem_SMS-Shenzhen_2025: Plastic cling films are widely used in food preservation but pose long-term environmental risks due to poor degradability, while microbial spoilage continues to cause significant food waste. To address these challenges, SMS-Shenzhen is designing a biodegradable and antimicrobial cling film using synthetic biology. We introduced the pls gene from Streptomyces albulus into Bacillus subtilis to enable ε-polylysine (PLL) production and introduced PPK2 and lysC311 to enhance the productivity. A kill switch is constructed by knocking out the alrA gene, rendering the strain auxotrophic and limiting its survival to controlled conditions. In parallel, we are developing a bilayer film by combining purified PLL with chitosan and sodium alginate-based materials. Our goal is to create a cling film that is both antimicrobial and biodegradable, offering a safer and more sustainable alternative to traditional plastic packaging.
igem_Jiangnan-China_2025: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe global public health threat, with drug-resistant bacteria increasingly endangering human health.The human antimicrobial peptide LL-37 offers a promising solution due to its high safety, low resistance potential, and immunomodulatory activity. Our project employs Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a chassis cell, integrating genetic engineering, fermentation optimization, and a D2P cell-free system to achieve high-yield biosynthesis of functional LL-37 at a significantly lower cost than chemical synthesis.We developed the CytoFlow platform, integrating biodynamic simulations, reinforcement learning, and diffusion models. This platform optimizes S. cerevisiae cultivation and designs LL-37 variants with superior antimicrobial performance. We also developed the EFUV-Cycle and RLAI-Cycle, and designed the educational game Cytopia Defense, the "Life Glow" bio-art activity, and the handbook Busting Rumors about Synthetic Biology to enhance the project's impact in both Integrated Human Practices and education.
igem_UAM_2025: Envenomation by venomous animals remains a global health concern, with scorpionism being particularly critical in Mexico, causing around 300,000 stings and around 1,400 deaths each year. Our project proposes an integrated three-system approach to address this issue. First, we aim to develop microbial production systems for recombinant antivenoms as sustainable and ethical alternatives to animal-derived ones. Second, we implement educational and social strategies to promote prevention and awareness within vulnerable communities. Third, we apply data modeling and optimization tools to improve healthcare logistics and accessibility in marginalized regions. Experimentally, we constructed an expression vector using the pPICZα backbone under AOX1 promoter control for expression in the Komagataella phaffii strain OPENPichia pep4 yps1. Alongside, our outreach and modeling efforts connect synthetic biology and community engagement, working toward a future where preventable deaths from scorpionism in Mexico are reduced as much as possible.
igem_BASIS-China_2025: Perfluoroalkyl and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) contamination is a global concern due to their persistence in water, widespread presence in daily life, and long-term health risks. Among them, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is the most prevalent and hazardous pollutant. By developing an integrated PFOA & fluoride ions biosensor, optimizing PFOA-degrading enzymes, and designing a systematic hardware platform, we aim to establish a PFOA governance system that integrates detection, biodegradation, and safe processing, providing a practical solution to mitigate environmental and health impacts.
igem_Guelph_2025: Project SeQUESTer aims to develop a sustainable, bioengineered filtration system to combat toxic heavy metal (THM) contamination in water, with an initial focus on lead (Pb). Lead pollution arises from industrial activity and aging infrastructure, posing persistent health and environmental hazards, especially in under-resourced communities. SeQUESTer introduces an innovative genetic sensing and sequestration platform using Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Our system integrates a riboswitch that detects lead ions, a reversible genetic memory switch that records exposure events, with the future direction to incorporate metal transporters that enhance cellular uptake and immobilization of lead. These engineered yeast cells are embedded within a porous agarose–zeolite scaffold housed in a scalable, modular biofiltration unit. This design enables simultaneous detection and removal of lead while maintaining environmental safety. SeQUESTer provides a low-cost, accessible, and eco-conscious alternative to conventional water treatment technologies.
igem_Lambert-GA_2025: 89,000 cases of Lyme disease were reported to the CDC in 2023, yet experts estimate that nearly half-a-million Americans are infected with Borrelia burgdorferi annually. This significant underdiagnosis is due to the rapid dissemination of the bacteria into tissue, causing current tests to rely on antibodies produced weeks post-infection. However, the outer surface protein, CspZ, persists in the bloodstream, allowing for early detection through LANCET. Our diagnostic workflow begins with proximity-dependent ligation to detect CspZ and produce DNA, which is then amplified by recombinase polymerase amplification. Cas12a targets this DNA, providing a user-friendly output through a lateral flow assay. Even with improved diagnosis, treatment continues to rely on antibiotics, contributing to antimicrobial resistance and failing to address post-treatment Lyme disease. LANCET offers a novel approach through a multiplexed CRISPR-interference system to silence critical genes, effectively killing the bacteria. Our initiative also includes community education, fostering proactive behaviors against Lyme.
igem_HKSSC_2025: Atopic Dermatitis (eczema) stems largely from filaggrin (FLG) mutations, causing skin barrier failure. Current treatments only manage inflammation. We propose synthesizing artificial FLG to directly repair the barrier, delivered via jojoba oil for optimal topical application. This targets the condition's root cause, the skin barrier dysfunction.
igem_GreatBay-SCIE_2025: Accounting for up to 20% of all respiratory allergy cases in humid areas, reaching a pervalence of around 30% in many countries around the world, indoors mold problem comprises one of the most serious threat to public health. To tackle this risk, GreatBay-SCIE 2025 devised a brand new mold killer, ArMOLDgeddon. Harnessing the antifungal properties of enzymes chitinase, glucanase, lysozyme and monoterpenoid geraniol, ArMOLDgeddon provides a safe and effective alternative to current mold removers. Chitinase and glucanase degrade critical structural polymers of the mold cell wall, while lysozyme magnifies the damage through cationic interaction with the cell wall components and disruption of fungal membranes. Geraniol, apart from furthering the attack on fungal membrane, provides a pleasant fragrance.  Furthermore, with the help of artificial intelligence and strong carbohydrate binding domains, ArMOLDgeddon evolves and improves, expediting towards the goal of the annihilation of mold-related diseases, and eradicating this pervasive global health threat.
igem_SJTU-BioX-Shanghai_2025: As the incidence of atopic dermatitis is increasing, the poor therapeutic experience of patients relying on long-term steroid use and immunosuppressants requires a breakthrough. Current treatments face a high recurrence rate. We stand to develop a more favorable treatment experience. Relevant studies have shown that the microbiome plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of atopic dermatitis, particularly the presence of Staphylococcus aureus and its inflammatory effects. Based on this, we designed a therapeutic system using engineered Staphylococcus epidermidis. We genetically modified Staphylococcus epidermidis to sense the AIP-C secreted by S. aureus and activate two downstream therapeutic pathways. The first pathway produces an nanobody that targets and neutralizes the inflammatory cytokine, while the second secretes AIP-C to suppress the virulence of S. aureus. Together, our system offers a safe and long-lasting therapeutic strategy, representing a paradigm shift in atopic dermatitis management - moving from symptom suppression to microbiome-mediated disease prevention.
igem_Evry-Paris-Saclay_2025: Billions of years ago, cyanobacteria transformed Earth’s atmosphere through carbon fixation, enabling the metabolic foundation of modern ecosystems. Yet, despite its central role, photosynthetic carbon fixation has not changed much since its origin. With SOLARIS, we reexamine this long-standing process from the perspective of synthetic biology, foundationally changing and advancing CO₂ fixation in cyanobacteria. Our solution lays the groundwork for photosynthesis 2.0 to overcome the kinetic and oxygen-sensitivity limitations of RuBisCO by introducing a distinct carbon fixation cycle supported by a carbonic anhydrase system we newly identified and confirmed for activity. This has the potential to make cyanobacteria far better at fixing CO₂ from the atmosphere and turning it into biomass. SOLARIS offers the tools and methodologies for rewriting core metabolic pathways with synthetic biology for optimizing synthetic carbon fixation cycles in vivo and in vitro, a foundational step toward programmable photosynthesis and a new generation of engineered phototrophs.
igem_Thessaly_2025: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) causes nearly half a million deaths worldwide each year, with incidence and mortality rates almost identical, reflecting the lack of effective treatments. To address this, we developed Clotho, a modular gene therapy designed to cure PDAC. Using an adeno-associated virus, we deliver a therapeutic transgene that activates exclusively in cancer cells. Once inside, it produces circular RNAs and the enzyme Cytosine Deaminase. The circular RNAs act as sponges for tumor-promoting miRNAs, enhancing cancer cell sensitivity to treatment. Meanwhile, the enzyme converts the harmless prodrug 5-fluorocytosine into the toxic compound 5-fluorouracil, selectively killing malignant cells. Complementing this, our software platform Kathesis generates patient-specific circular RNA sequences based on individual genetic profiles. This dual approach enables precise, personalized, and targeted therapy, reducing off-target effects and introducing a novel strategy to overcome drug resistance in PDAC and potentially other diseases.
igem_Thailand-RIS_2025: Thailand ranked sixth in the world for mismanaged plastic waste, sending over a million tonnes into the oceans each year (Labcom et al., 2024). Microplastics are now found throughout the country’s ecosystems—from marine animals to water, air, and farmland—threatening wildlife, food safety, and human health (Chanpiwat, 2021). The most common culprit is polyethylene terephthalate (PET), making up 37% of poorly managed waste. In 2016, scientists discovered PETase, an enzyme from Ideonella sakaiensis that can break down PET. However, such microbial hosts are inefficient, unsafe, and unsustainable. Therefore, the Thailand‑RIS iGEM 2025 team explored a different approach—producing PETase in plants—of which we present the first successful demonstration. Although stable transformation is still underway, we achieved transient expression of PETase fused with an alpha‑amylase 3S signal peptide in Nicotiana benthamiana, resulting in extracellular secretion. This proof of concept lays the groundwork for scalable, sustainable plant-based strategies against forever-increasing plastic pollution.
igem_HUBU-WuHan_2025: Arsenic contamination in rice paddies threatens food safety and environmental health. Traditional large-instrument-based monitoring is costly and unsuitable for on-site rapid screening. To solve this, our project develops a novel arsenic biosensor via the "niche-matching" principle, sourcing key elements from Cupriavidus metallidurans CML2 (a rice endophyte adapted to paddies). We construct an "AND-gate-like" genetic circuit with a split-GFP system to reduce basal leakage and boost signal-to-noise ratio, and optimize performance through multiple "Design-Build-Test-Learn" (DBTL) cycles for sensitive, specific arsenic detection. This biosensor enables on-site paddy arsenic monitoring and lays a foundation for future "detection-remediation" microbial agents, aiding sustainable agriculture and environmental protection.
igem_Barcelona-UB_2025: As synthetic biology positions itself as a field of the future, the need for new tools that allow better control of protein expression and new options for genetic engineering is clear. SKIPPIT is a platform that harnesses the full power of STOP Codon Readthrough elements, from both characterising them to making them into a tool: a first-in-class readthrough riboswitch.  STOP Codon Readthrough elements interact with the ribosome at the STOP codon site, leading to the STOP codon being decoded by a tRNA instead of the termination complex, allowing translation to continue beyond the STOP.  Designing this switch has only been possible thanks to the development of a cutting edge Software: TADPOLE. This software uses computationally-predicted RNA structures to optimise the design of RNA switches from just two RNA sequences.
igem_BIT_2025: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death globally. Despite advances in chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, treatment remains limited by drug resistance and toxicity. This study presents the “CRC-killer in and out” integrated delivery kit, combining endogenous oral capsules with engineered bacteria and exogenous intelligent microneedle patches for comprehensive CRC therapy. The “in” module enhances intestinal targeting and bioavailability via peptide-mediated accumulation, while the “out” module employs minimally invasive microneedles with iontophoresis-enhanced transdermal delivery and responsive drug release. Together, they enable individualized administration, improved compliance, and non-professional usability. The dual-path system merges home-use convenience with scalable applicability, reducing medical burdens， which offer an innovative approach for CRC home-based and large-scale treatment.
igem_KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei_2025: Greenhouse gas emission is a major factor driving climate change. Considering the limitations of conventional mitigation approaches, our team proposed a synthetic biology approach by genetically modifying cyanobacteria Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 to enhance CO2 fixation efficiency. Our strategy involves overexpressing the cmpAB and CD fusion genes containing a light-sensitive promoter to increase the amount of bicarbonate transporter 1 (BCT1) within the cyanobacterial carbon concentrating mechanism (CCM). Ultimately, we aim to increase inorganic carbon uptake and saturate RuBisCO’s CO2 binding sites, facilitating photosynthetic CO2 sequestration. Coupling protein modeling and functional assays performed on wild-type cyanobacteria to obtain a dry lab model quantifying the cyanobacterial carbon intake, we envision integrating the engineered cyanobacteria into a carbon fixation photobioreactor. In addition, besides evaluating the scalability and sustainability of our hardware from a scientific and economic perspective, we also extended our outreach into the local and global community by educating about synthetic biology.
igem_BAID-China_2025: Pesticide residues on food pose serious health risks to the whole world, yet current detection methods remain inefficient and unstable. Recognizing this issue, we developed Pestacheck, a rapid, low-cost pesticide residue detection test strip based on the enzyme-inhibition principle of acetylcholinesterase (AChE). Through Alanine-scanning mutagenesis, we engineered AChE mutants via Cell-Free expression system. The optimized enzyme was immobilized with Gold Nanoparticles (AuNP) to improve sensitivity and integrated into a colloidal gold-based test strip for visible colorimetric detection. Together, Pestacheck provides a user-friendly synthetic biology solution for on-site pesticide residue detection.
igem_KCISLK-Taiwan_2025: Food waste has a huge impact on our planet. It destroys habitats, emits huge amounts of greenhouse gases, and threatens society deeply. Currently, one of the most sustainable methods is using black soldier fly larvae to degrade food waste. However, black soldier fly larvae are unable to efficiently digest cellulose, suggesting that improving the degradation process could enhance overall conversion efficiency and lower the costs associated with food waste treatment. LarVase aims to mass-produce endo-1,4-β-glucanase, a cellulase originating from Bacillus subtilis, through cloning into an E. coli BL21 expression vector. With our specially designed plasmids, we used YebF, a carrier protein having a similar function as a signal peptide, to be able to transport endo-1,4-β-glucanase outside the cell. This will lower the current costs of enzyme production while maintaining environmental sustainability.
igem_HK-Joint-School_2025: PestiGuard is an innovative biosensor that puts food safety directly into the hands of consumers. To address the global health risks from pesticide residues, we have developed a simple, on-site detection system. At its heart are engineered bacteria containing a specialized RNA aptamer. When a specific pesticide is present, it binds to the aptamer, suppressing a fluorescent reporter gene and resulting in a dimmer glow. This provides an intuitive visual signal: brighter means safer, dimmer means contaminated. For precise results, we created companion software and hardware. A photo of the test sample is instantly analyzed, comparing the color intensity to a safety reference to display clear contamination levels. By integrating synthetic biology with smart technology, PestiGuard transforms complex lab testing into an accessible, user-friendly process, empowering everyone to make informed decisions about their food.
igem_GU-Frankfurt_2025: Fungal pathogens pose a major threat to agriculture, causing significant economic losses and straining global food systems. Climate change worsens these challenges by creating warmer, more humid conditions that favor fungal infections. Conventional fungicides often harm beneficial organisms, disrupt ecosystems, and drive pathogen resistance, threatening long-term food security. We propose a more precise and sustainable alternative. Using a modular sensor system with a genetic AND-gate, our engineered bacteria detect pathogen-specific signals tied to physiology and secretome, releasing antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) only when needed. This ensures targeted action while minimizing off-target effects. SPROUT is a scalable, precision-based platform for next-generation plant protection. Its modular design allows easy adaptation to diverse crops and pathogens, enabling efficient, on-demand AMP release. By combining specificity, adaptability, and sustainability, SPROUT offers a practical and innovative approach to strengthening agricultural resilience against fungal diseases.
igem_Science Tokyo_2025: We developed Xylego, an engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 designed as a low-burden synbiotic therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). Xylego integrates three key modules: (1) Colonization support – enables selective growth using xylitol, reducing administration frequency; (2) Mucosal healing – secretes epidermal growth factor (EGF) to promote epithelial repair and break the inflammatory cycle; and (3) Inflammation-dependent kill switch – a tetrathionate-sensing restriction–modification system that self-destructs after inflammation resolves, preventing long-term risks and antibiotic gene transfer. Xylego is expected to enhance remission rates, improve adherence, and provide a safe, adaptable platform for patient-tailored probiotic therapies.
igem_IIT-Bombay_2025: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) forms biofilms that protect bacterial cells and confer strong resistance to antibiotics, making them a major cause of chronic and persistent infections. These infections are particularly harmful in immunocompromised patients, exacerbating conditions such as cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs). Staphylococcus epidermidis (S. epidermidis), a common skin commensal, secretes an extracellular serine protease (Esp) capable of cleaving autolysin, an essential factor in biofilm formation responsible for extracellular DNA (eDNA) release, which enhances biofilm stability. However, Esp also targets human biofilm components and other host proteins, limiting its therapeutic potential. To make Esp a viable therapeutic agent, it must selectively cleave bacterial biofilm proteins—specifically, autolysin—without degrading human substrates. To achieve this, we aim to engineer Esp through site-directed mutagenesis (SDM) to enhance its substrate specificity toward the autolysin. By introducing targeted mutations based on Esp–autolysin (Atl) interaction analyses, we seek to reduce its off-target activity against human proteins while maintaining its biofilm-degrading capability, enabling its safe use as an anti-biofilm therapeutic.
igem_TUDarmstadt_2025: Mars has long fascinated humankind. With the growing interest in its exploration, the use of local resources, especially water, is becoming increasingly important. However, its huge natural water resources are contaminated by toxic perchlorate salts and thus unusable.  Therefore, we engineer Bacillus subtilis 168 to detoxify perchlorate fully and convert it into harmless chloride and oxygen. To measure perchlorate concentrations, we established an in vivo perchlorate quantification assay that functions via organic phase extraction.  To understand the underlying biochemistry, we characterized perchlorate degradation enzymes in vitro and investigated the effect of rational mutations to improve their performance.  To enable practical implementation of our project, we built and tested a low-cost DIY anaerobic bioreactor. In order to simulate Martian microgravity, we designed, built and verified a random positioning machine from scratch. This device enables biological studies in simulated microgravity environments.
igem_Sorbonne University_2025: Nereis' project focuses on conserving the marine environment by degrading the pollutant naphthalene, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We identified salt-tolerant genes encoding proteins that help organisms survive in high sodium environments, as well as a catabolic pathway that uses naphthalene as a carbon source. Our goal is to genetically modify Pseudomonas putida, to be both salt-tolerant and capable of enhanced naphthalene degradation. These modification would allow the bacteria to function effectively in marine conditions. The naphthalene degradation pathway is found in P.putida G7, specifically in the NAH7 plasmid, which encodes the necessary degrading enzymes. Major challenges include adapting P. putida to high sodium concentration and introducing the large NAH7 plasmid. First, we will modified the bacteria with salt tolerant genes and test its tolerance to different sodium concentration. Second, we want to introduce the degrading enzymes in the salt-tolerant strain and assess the effectiveness of naphthalene degradation.
igem_XJTLU-Science-China_2025: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive subtype, with rapid progression, poor prognosis, and no effective targeted therapies, highlighting urgent need for new strategies.  Building on Prof. Shang Cai’s work on intracellular commensal bacteria—especially the tumor-targeting potential of Staphylococcus—we developed TroGen, an intracellular delivery platform using engineered commensals. To enhance invasion, we introduced the `fnbA` gene into non-pathogenic Staphylococcus to express S. aureus FnBPA, exploiting integrin-mediated endocytosis for efficient TNBC entry. Two biosafety modules confine bacterial survival and therapeutic payload expression to the tumor microenvironment.  Using AlphaFold-Multimer, MD, MM/PBSA, and phylogenetic analysis, we selected the optimal FnBP from multiple candidates. We formulated a reaction–diffusion–convection coupled PDE and used COMSOL Multiphysics to simulate intratumoral bacterial diffusion.  Human Practices informed iterative design, and outreach activities fostered scientific curiosity.
igem_Sustech-Med_2025: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive, hypoxic tumor microenvironment (TME) dominated by M2 macrophages. To address this, we engineered the probiotic E. coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) as a targeted living therapeutic. Our engineered auxotrophic EcN strain incorporates two synthetic genetic circuits: a hypoxia-responsive plasmid for tumor-specific production of the STING agonist c-di-GMP, and a synthetic "suicide" circuit for AHL-inducible bacterial lysis and payload release with essential metabolic gene thyA and dapA knockout. This triple system ensures precise immune activation within the tumor and provides a crucial biocontainment mechanism. We further developed a mathematical model to simulate AHL diffusion and its kinetic relationship with therapy, and designed a gut-on-a-chip device for physiologically relevant testing. This work establishes a safe, modular platform for targeted CRC immunotherapy.
igem_SHSBNU-China_2025: Space exploration requires lightweight and durable materials to be manufactured in situ. Current chemical-based materials rely heavily on Earth supply chains. To address this gap, we engineered fusion proteins combining hagfish intermediate filament (HIF) and mussel foot protein (MFP) domains. Expression was induced in E. coli BL21 (DE3) and proteins were purified using Ni–NTA column. The best estimated yield reached 193 mg/ml. Co-assembly showed hydrogel formation, and the adhesive performance quantified by maximum force measurement recorded strength near 20,000 N/m², comparable to commercial glues. Adhesion was strong at space walking temperature (120 °C) but rapidly decline when below –20 °C. We developed SHIELD—a 3D-printed, low-cost fermentation device achieving cell densities upto OD600~20. Besides, we modified the fusion protein's structure, removing one of the terminal domains, and explored the structure-property relationships with preliminary results. With ARMOR, we are excited for the potential of syn-bio for next-generation space materials.
igem_HK-HCY-PCMS_2025: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, characterized by progressive optic nerve damage and often asymptomatic until significant vision loss occurs. Current treatments primarily address elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) but fail to halt the underlying retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration. To address this dual pathology, we developed a novel, non-invasive eye drop formulation containing two fusion peptides: FT, which lowers IOP, and BC, which provides neuroprotection by reducing RGC apoptosis. This dual-therapy approach simultaneously targets both key disease mechanisms, offering a more comprehensive strategy to slow glaucoma progression. Our project integrated human practices to ensure viability and societal impact. We engaged patients, clinicians, and bioethicists to refine our work ethically. Through stakeholder dialogue and targeted outreach, we balanced diverse needs and raised glaucoma awareness. This created a positive feedback loop, strengthening our project's purpose and laying the groundwork for future innovation.
igem_Brno Czech Republic_2025: Dairy farmers are struggling to keep their farms profitable - the protein feed, the most crucial element, is also one of the most expensive components for them. The most popular protein source is soybean. It contributed to the loss of natural ecosystems in Brazil's tropical savanna. Duckweed, the fastest-growing plant on Earth, contains as much protein as soybeans and grows 10x faster. It is set to provide an affordable protein source for every farm. But duckweed, as promising as it looks, cannot match 3000 years of selective breeding of soybeans. To make it a crop, we need SynBio. We are developing a method for 5x faster genetic engineering of duckweed, constructing an autonomous cultivation system and a yield prediction model, simplifying the scaling of duckweed. The first steps toward unlocking the massive potential of this tiny plant… To save farmers' money, the Cerrado savanna, and to make plants truly scalable.
igem_Fudan_2025: DR. sTraTeGY is built on "Grape Yeast" chassis, designed to track fungal drug resistance mutations. It transforms the evolution of fungi from a static snapshot into an observable spatio-temporal lineage tree. Its current version has two functions: mutation event recording and cell lineage tracing. Our optimized transcription unit - pSTM1-driven EMSfp499, combines a mutation-sensitive promoter with an EMS-resistant fluorescent protein, enabling high-fidelity recording of mutation dynamics. We developed YeastVerse, a modeling and simulation tool, to predict key parameters such as fluorescent protein expression and maturation, which allows dry-lab simulation to guide subsequent wet-lab experiments. In addition, we have established a DBTL cycle that integrates mathematical modeling with AI-assisted reasoning.   We engage rare disease communities, through collaborative art and sensory-inclusive activities, fostering an accessible and participatory scientific environment. By integrating synthetic biology, computing, and community engagements, DR. sTraTeGY provides a new strategy to address the global challenge of fungal drug resistance.
igem_NWU-CHINA-C_2025: Type III collagen (COLIII) not only supports tissue elasticity but also regulates the tumor microenvironment by transmitting dormancy signals to cancer cells. To overcome the limitations of animal-derived collagen, we established a synthetic-biology-based microbial production system to produce humanized COLIII, achieving biosafety and functional customization. By introducing the GVMGFO motif, a specific binding site for Discoidin Domain Receptor 1 (DDR1), we engineered COLIII to precisely target DDR1 on tumor cell surfaces. Using molecular modeling, docking, and dynamics simulations, we selected the recombinant COLIII variant (rCOL III) with the most stable structure and highest binding affinity for DDR1.The selected rCOL III was successfully expressed in Pichia pastoris and showed preliminary intervention effects on breast cancer cells in vitro, demonstrating a potential inhibitory role. This project integrates synthetic biology, protein engineering, and computational design, providing a green and modular biomaterial strategy for breast cancer intervention and prevention.
igem_MIT-MAHE_2025: Pepper foot rot is a devastating disease that affects black pepper (P. nigrum) vines. Caused by the oomycete Phytophthora capsici, the infection leads to extensive yield loss and mortality in Karnataka and Kerala. Globally, plantations in Vietnam and Indonesia also suffer a similar fate. Chemical fungicides and current biocontrol measures are ineffective and unsustainable, driving the need for an innovative solution.  MIT-MAHE has developed a targeted, preventative solution that curbs foot rot. PhytClub implements small interfering RNA (siRNA) that are specifically designed to silence the bZIP transcription factor in P. capsici, through the RNA interference mechanism. Chitosan nanoparticles encapsulate the siRNA to confer stability and aid their uptake into the pathogen. Furthermore, the team has automated the siRNA design process and combined it with a model that predicts the stability of an siRNA-nanoparticle complex, providing a foundational software tool that helps future researchers seamlessly build gene silencing systems.
igem_WHU-China_2025: Biological computing holds great promise, yet past engineered bacterial circuits for logic gates have suffered from excessive complexity, cumbersome operation, and reliance on multiple input substances. Our LOGIC project overcomes these problems by developing a novel approach to constructing a biocomputer—utilizing quorum sensing and spatial diffusion to form logic gates. For addition calculation, we construct high-pass and band-pass genetic circuits based on the quorum sensing (QS) system. Through the diffusion of QS molecules in solid media, we can build various logic gates and connect them to perform multi-bit binary calculations. For repetitive operation, we engineer a light-induced QS molecule degradation enzyme and a protein degradation tag to refresh the calculator. Building upon the calculator, we can also build accessories like result storage, decimal result display and latches, demonstrating its extensive prospects. Furthermore, we construct a LOGIC Toolkit with visualization software for future research.
igem_UCAS-China_2025: Early detection of plant pathogens is essential for reducing crop losses, yet most diagnostic systems remain laboratory-bound. We developed PROTATO: Proteolysis-based Detection for Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato Affected Tomato, a cell-free and protein logic–based biosensing platform enabling on-site pathogen detection. PROTATO integrates a coiled-coil–mediated chain exchange reaction as its molecular logic core and a dual-input AND gate that responds specifically to the pathogen effector AvrRpt2 protease and the phytotoxin coronatine (COR), reconstituting split luciferase, GFP, or trehalase reporters. A positive-feedback loop amplifies protease activity, improving detection sensitivity and signal strength. To enable field deployment, we engineered the PROTATO KIT, a 3D-printed electrochemical device that converts glucose signals into electronic readouts via glucose oxidase–modified electrodes and microcontrollers. Portable (Air) and scalable (Pro) versions support diverse agricultural applications. Our project establishes a generalizable framework for cell-free protein logic, advancing low-cost biosensing for crop protection and beyond.
igem_Alma_2025: Pseudogymnoascus destructans is a pathogenic fungus that causes White-nose syndrome (WNS), one of the most devastating wildlife diseases in modern history, responsible for mass bat mortality across North America. Locally in Michigan, 5 of our 9 bat species are affected--with repercussions for biodiversity, agriculture, public health, and environmental stability. WNS develops in bats during their hibernation period when proteolytic enzymes produced by the fungus degrade the collagen in their nose, ears, and wings, causing them to wake prematurely from wintertime hibernation, leading to energy depletion, lethargy, and death by starvation due to the lack of necessary resources in winter. There are no effective treatments currently. We propose engineering Escherichia coli to secrete serine protease inhibitor(s) targeting the virulence factor of the fungus. These inhibitors would block collagen degradation, allowing bats to maintain uninterrupted hibernation, thus improving survival outcomes for one of our most essential, if silent allies.
igem_TU-Delft_2025: Snaccine is a novel type of vaccine, ideal for vaccinating chickens against avian influenza (bird flu). Genetically modified bacteriophages are taken orally, in a stomach acid-resistant pill. They reproduce inside gut bacteria, while also producing RNA packaged within armour (an MS2 virus-like particle coated with cell-penetrating peptides). This RNA enters (eukaryotic) host cells and works just like an mRNA vaccine, tricking the cell into producing an antigen. This antigen is detected by the immune system and teaches it to recognise and fight the original pathogen. Snaccines share many of the same advantages that mRNA technology has over traditional vaccines. But where typical mRNA vaccines have to be kept in freezers, Snaccines can be stored and transported at room temperature. Together with their cheaper production and oral administration route, Snaccine is an ideal technology for fighting bird flu.
igem_Nanjing-China_2025: This project addresses the critical challenges of drug resistance and systemic toxicity in conventional cancer therapy by developing a novel live bacterial delivery system based on an engineered Serratia marcescens strain. We leveraged the native capacity of this bacterium to synthesize prodigiosin—a potent antitumor compound—while implementing biosafety enhancements through msbB gene knockout to reduce endotoxin production. For precise tumor targeting, we functionalized the attenuated strain with carboxymethyl cellulose encapsulation and the KP101 homing peptide. To support quantitative analysis and predictive modeling, we developed a comprehensive computational toolkit including an automated fluorescence image segmentation pipeline, a ConvLSTM-based spatiotemporal prediction model, and the integrated OncoPredict Suite platform. Guided by responsible innovation and the SEEK framework, our project combines synthetic biology with translational tool development to offer a targeted and adaptable strategy for next-generation cancer treatment
igem_Lund_2025: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), the main component of polyester textiles, dominates global fiber production and generates millions of tons of waste annually. Current recycling methods rely on energy-intensive chemical processes. Our project, Trashformers, tackles this challenge by developing a synthetic biology system for PET textile recycling and upcycling, designed to provide all the reaction components needed for efficient depolymerization and upcycling. We focus on enzymatic glycolysis to depolymerize PET into bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), a monomer suited for re-polymerization. To achieve this, we designed a system based on E. coli BL21(DE3) and devices utilizing PETase hydrolases. We design two complementary systems in parallel. The first employs enzymatic hydrolysis to degrade PET into terephthalic acid (TPA), and ethylene glycol required for subsequent glycolysis. The second uses rational enzyme design to create a novel enzyme that activates TPA with coenzyme A  Paving the way for PET upcycling through metabolic and chemical valorization.
igem_DKU_2025: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons, leading to motor impairments such as tremors and rigidity. Current treatments rely on L-DOPA supplementation, but long-term use results in decreased efficacy and severe side effects. To address these limitations, we propose engineering Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S. cerevisiae) to biosynthesize and regulate L-DOPA production using the yeast codon-optimized CYP76AD6 gene from Beta vulgaris partnered with the AR2 gene from Arabidopsis thaliana. By integrating metabolic engineering and synthetic biology, our system aims to improve L-DOPA bioavailability while reducing treatment-related complications. The system incorporates sophisticated feedback mechanisms to maintain optimal L-DOPA levels, offering a potentially groundbreaking approach to PD therapy.
igem_ULaval_2025: Antimicrobial resistance is currently a major global health crisis. To counter this issue, alternatives to antibiotics must be developed. One promising strategy involves the use of siderophores, iron-chelating molecules naturally synthesized by bacteria. We aimed to hack this system by adding a gold nanoparticle to one of Klebsiella pneumoniae’s siderophores, aerobactin. These nanoparticles can then be activated with NIR lasers to kill bacteria. Our team focused on cloning aerobactin in Escherichia coli. We also performed in silico analyses to optimize aerobactin biosynthesis and deepen our understanding of the siderophore’s internalization by K. pneumoniae. A genome-scale metabolic analysis of aerobactin’s citrate production, along with biomolecular modeling of the TonB-dependent transporter embedded in the gram-negative bacterial membrane, was conducted. The next steps of this project would involve the synthesis of gold nanoparticles followed by their conjugation with aerobactin.
igem_ICJFLS_2025: The core components of rose essential oil are geraniol and citronellol, while that of lavender is linalool. These three components share highly similar terpenoid biosynthetic pathways. This commonality provides us with an unprecedented technical opportunity: by modifying microbial cell factories, we enable yeast to produce geraniol (the common precursor substance) and Escherichia coli to synthesize citronellol and linalool. By enhancing the supply of precursor substances and introducing selective catalytic enzymes, we construct a metabolic network that can efficiently synthesize geraniol, citronellol, and linalool. The key lies in the introduction of regulatable promoter systems and artificial gene circuits, which allow for precise regulation of the metabolic flux of each synthetic branch through external induction and culture parameters. This enables end-users to dynamically adjust the synthesis rate of each component according to their personal preferences, and ultimately obtain personalized mixed essential oil components in a single fermentation system at one time.
igem_IIT-Madras_2025: Targeted DNA methylation is a promising approach for programmable gene regulation. To explore this, we designed and expressed a novel fusion protein, dCas9-Dam (DNA adenine methyltransferase), in E. coli. dCas9 was directed to user-specified loci with the help of guide RNA, enabling targeted adenine methylation at GATC sites. We constructed a plasmid encoding dCas9-Dam with guide RNA and a reporter plasmid containing a GFP gene downstream of a methylation-sensitive promoter. Co-transfection into E. coli allowed us to assess whether dCas9-Dam could induce targeted methylation and regulate GFP expression. Our results will test the ability of dCas9-Dam to perform locus-specific DNA methylation and alter reporter gene expression.The system can be extended to other methyltransferases in bacteria, opening avenues for applications in biomanufacturing, therapeutics, and diagnostics. By enabling precise epigenetic editing, this approach holds potential for developing novel treatments for diseases linked to aberrant methylation, such as cancer, neurodegenerative disorders,and imprinting-related syndromes
igem_PennState_2025: Heparosan is a key polysaccharide precursor in the synthesis of heparin, an essential anticoagulant widely used in medicine. However, current methods of heparosan production rely on inefficient microbial strains. Our project aims to design and optimize synthesis of heparosan in a more commonly used strain - BL21 (DE3). We are reconstructing the heparosan synthesis pathway found in E. coli K5 by expressing four essential genes—kfiA, kfiB, kfiC, and kfiD, and inserting them onto a single plasmid, incorporating a library of degenerate ribosome binding sites (RBS) on our primers. Using degenerate DNA sequences for our RBS allows us to synthesize a library of varying ribosomal binding affinity for each gene, which in turn, gives us a wide range of gene expression. This allows us to determine the optimal activity level for each gene to produce the most heparosan.
igem_DBHS-CA_2025: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a chronic condition characterized by inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. The cause of IBD is an overreactive immune response, leading to prolonged inflammation and tissue damage. A key regulator of such inflammation, Interleukin-10 (IL-10), plays a fundamental role in modulating inflammation and maintaining cell homeostasis by protecting the body from an uncontrolled immune response by inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6. However, IL-10’s therapeutic potential is severely limited by its structural instability due to its homodimer nature and easy degradation within the body. This instability reduces its effectiveness as a long-term treatment leaving patients with limited options for prolonged IBD treatments. To address this issue, we propose a probiotic-based approach, engineering a mutated more stable form of Il-10 (MIL-10). Delivered through dairy products like yogurt, this system would provide MIL-10 production in reaction to pro-inflammatory cytokines, ensuring sustained inflammation control for diseases like IBD.
igem_Washington_2025: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a pathogenic bacterium that is responsible for an estimated 7% of all healthcare-associated infections. Exotoxin A (ETA) is one major virulence factor of PA. As a result, therapeutics targeting the inhibition of ETA activity are under development. ETA enters human cells through the CD91 receptor, activates via furin cleavage, and modifies eukaryotic elongation factor 2, inhibiting protein synthesis and inducing apoptosis. Although some inhibitors show signs of success, they consist of either small-molecule inhibitors, which have significant off-target effects, or antibodies, which cannot be produced efficiently due to size and folding properties. To address these limitations, we utilize RF diffusion, Protein MPNN, and AlphaFold to create a protein inhibitor that binds specifically to ETA's receptor binding domain. We tested these computationally designed inhibitors by expressing and purifying them, assessing their binding affinity to ETA and evaluating their ability to prevent ETA-mediated cell death using cell-based assays.
igem_TAU-Israel_2025: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and many patients still lack effective long-term treatment options. Oncoligo introduces a modular therapeutic platform that harnesses antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to selectively silence essential cancer genes within a synthetic-lethality framework, enabling the targeting of tumor-suppressor-driven and intracellular cancers. Our computational pipeline integrates molecular dynamics, machine learning, and algorithmic optimization to design all parts of the platform. We specifically design potent ASOs, which are conjugated to antibodies for targeted delivery. Within each antibody, tumor-associated epitopes stimulate immune activation and memory. Experimentally, our designed ASOs outperform commercial ones, showing superior knockdown at the mRNA, protein, and cellular levels. In parallel, we optimized antibody expression systems and developed a dedicated software tool that facilitates ASO design across diverse genes and organisms. By uniting synthetic biology, computation, and entrepreneurship, Oncoligo pioneers a versatile, scalable framework for precision oncology - redefining how we treat cancer.
igem_UCSC_2025: In order to address the global challenge of mycotoxin contamination in food and drink products, we aim to develop a detoxification system adaptable to diverse agricultural communities and food systems worldwide. Our methods focus on aflatoxin B1, the most carcinogenic mycotoxin and a major burden to resource-limited communities. Once bound, toxins can be removed through simple, inexpensive, and widely available cellulose-based materials that can be safely composted after use. As part of the plasmid design process, we introduce NOODL (Novel Optimization Of DNA Linkers), a Julia-based genetic algorithm that generates custom spacer sequences for single-stranded DNA. This tool simplifies spacer design by minimizing unwanted interactions and secondary structures between functional ssDNA components for synthetic biology applications. By combining computational design and genetic engineering, our work offers an impactful approach to improving food safety while providing adaptable tools that foster innovation across synthetic biology.
igem_Outaouais_2025: By 2050, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is expected to kill 10 million people each year, making it a major global threat. Here in Québec, our farmers follow strict rules for antibiotic use—they require a vet’s prescription. Even with these measures, resistant bacteria still emerge, particularly in manure and wastewater. When we started our One Health Outaouais (OHO) project, our plan was to develop a test for AMR genes to map the region’s resistome. But conversations with farmers, veterinarians, and experts helped us realize our approach was too academic. They didn’t need more data; they needed practical tools to make better, faster decisions for their animals. So, we transformed our test into a product: the VIGIL | FARM platform. VIGIL | FARM will provide farmers with on-site rapid diagnostics and reliable information, helping them use antibiotics more precisely and only when necessary — protecting both animal health and public safety.
igem_Virginia_2025: The effects of climate change underscore the need to develop sustainable energy technology. Hydrogen (H2) based sustainable energy solutions decarbonize high-heat industrial processes and long-distance transport. However, current H2 production is land and water-intensive, and largely reliant on fossil fuels. Dark Fermentation (DF)—an anaerobic process where glucose is converted to H2—is a sustainable alternative that can be integrated into waste-to-energy (WTE) streams. Currently, DF cannot produce H2 in commercially viable quantities. Our device, “The Cysteinator”, solves this challenge by supplementing DF bioreactor feedstocks with precise concentrations of L-cysteine.
